ko-news-notices-374-8372c75064.title: Ten East Sea undersea feature names accepted by an international subcommittee
ko-news-notices-374-8372c75064.text:
Ten East Sea undersea feature names accepted by an international subcommittee
2022-03-02
Ten East Sea undersea feature names accepted by an international subcommittee
The name “Jeon Jae-gyu Seamount” is also being listed internationally
Ten undersea feature names in the East Sea are to be listed after being accepted by the subcommittee.
The government announced on the 11th that the 20th meeting of the Sub-Committee on Undersea Feature Names (SCUFN), which had been under way in Monaco since the 9th, had decided to accept all 10 names for East Sea undersea features proposed by Korea on the 10th of the previous month.
Korea is also expected to strengthen its international standing and expand its influence over future additions of undersea feature names by hosting the 21st SCUFN meeting, scheduled for the first half of next year.
The East Sea feature names accepted by SCUFN this time include “Gangwon Plateau,” “Ulleung Plateau,” “Usan Trough,” “Usan Escarpment,” “Onnuri Basin,” “Saenal Basin,” “Hupo Bank,” “Kiminu Seamount,” “Igyuwon Ridge,” and “Anyongbok Seamount.”
This was the first time since international naming procedures began in 1974 that an East Sea undersea feature name in a Korean form had been accepted by an international organization. The government expected this to lead to the names being included in the international gazetteer of undersea feature names and widely used as international standards.
The government also announced that an undersea feature named for the late Jeon Jae-gyu, a member of the Korean Antarctic team who died while participating in a rescue operation in Maxwell Bay during research work at King Sejong Station in Antarctica in 2003, would be listed as well.
The name is “Jeon Jae-gyu Seamount.” The feature was first discovered by a U.S. geological research team (Dr. E. Domack, a professor at Hamilton College); it was named by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names last year and is now being registered with an international organization.
The government plans to continue discovering and naming undersea features in Korean waters and, through further submissions, promote the international use of more Korean undersea feature names.

ko-news-notices-375-8372c75064.title: 2017 Korea
ko-news-notices-375-8372c75064.text:
2017 Korea
2022-03-02
What will our society look like in 2017? Anyone who wants to look ahead to the next 10 years can draw an overall picture by looking at what changes we and society have experienced over the past 10 years, that is, over the 10 years since 1997, when the foreign exchange crisis hit.
There are a lot of stories about rapid change or a rapidly changing environment, but it would be more correct to imagine a gradually changed future that is fully predictable rather than a drastically changed future that is disconnected from the present. No one can accurately predict the future, but in this article, we will carefully summarize important trends that can characterize the future based on the present.
First, the impact of changes in population composition on the growth rate of the Korean economy will become increasingly clear. In other words, a decline in the potential growth rate will not be avoidable, and the Korean economy is expected to gradually lose dynamism, and the variables that have the greatest impact on this can be found in the increase in the elderly population and the decrease in the productive population.
At the end of 2006, the Korea Development Institute published a report titled ‘Economic and Social Ripple Effects of Aging Population Structure and Response Tasks.’ This report forecasts Korea's potential growth rate from 2003 to 2050, predicting that Korea will continue to transform into a low-growth country with 2.91% in the 2020s, 1.60% in the 2030s, and 0.74% in the 2040s. Considering that the potential growth rate in the 2010s was 4%, the growth rate is expected to drop to almost zero percent over the next 30 years.
Of course, there are variables depending on the increasing trend of immigration, unification of the Korean Peninsula, and the direction of institutional reform, but it seems inevitable that the potential growth rate will gradually decline over the next 10 years. Korea's first baby-boom cohort, born from 1958 through 1962, totaled as many as 5 million. By 2015 and 2020, when retirement among this cohort was expected to be well under way, the share of the population aged 65 and older was projected to rise to 12.9% and 15.6%, respectively. By contrast, the share of people aged 14 and older was projected to fall to 13.7% and 12.4%, respectively. The previous year's figures for people aged 65 and older and those under 14 were 9.5% and 18.6%, respectively. These figures give an overall picture of the changing population mix, and the coming decade would be when its effect on economic growth became visible.
Second, the rapid growth of China's economic power will have an impact on all aspects of Korean society, and the impact on manufacturing will be especially evident. The future is currently in progress. The 10 years that the Korean manufacturing industry will face can be inferred from the following article by Beijing-based correspondent Heo Min, which reports on the recent status of the Chinese automobile industry.
“Low-priced Chinese small cars costing around 6 million won each will enter the U.S. market beginning in 2008. Built with American technology, they are much better in quality than existing Chinese cars, yet they are inexpensive because they use low-cost labor and could become ‘Korean-car killers.’ On July 4 in Beijing, Chrysler President Tom LaSorda, of the United States’ third-largest automaker, signed an agreement to jointly develop small cars with Yin Tongyao, chairman of Chery, China’s largest domestic automaker. Chery also signed an export contract with the European market that day.”
Many manufacturing companies that make and sell mediocre products at mediocre prices will experience difficulties and be caught up in the midst of restructuring. Localization strategies, such as moving manufacturing companies to China, India, and other third countries for survival, are expected to gain further momentum. As a result, unless special circumstances develop, it appears that it will become increasingly difficult to significantly reduce the growth rate and unemployment rate in Korean society. This is expected to further worsen the employment situation for young people who do not have special skills or knowledge and have difficulty finding jobs in overseas markets, and this phenomenon itself is expected to further worsen the phenomenon of low growth and high unemployment.
The automobile industry is a symbolic sector of Korean manufacturing. I believe that the automobile industry suggests the future that Korea's manufacturing industry will face. Fortunately, if a groundbreaking change can occur in labor-management relations, the situation may be reversed, but as long as the current situation continues, the sandwich situation and crisis theory in the Korean manufacturing industry is likely to receive further strength.
On the other hand, the biggest beneficiaries of Chinese industry will be Korean consumers. Korean consumers are expected to enjoy the positive effects of cheap Chinese products.
Third, it is highly likely that society as a whole will experience an increased sense of crisis and an awakening to innovation in the next 10 years. Therefore, if Korea succeeds in choosing a leader who properly reads the changes of the times and has the driving force, Korea can succeed in an unexpected change and innovation project. This could help bring about a major improvement in Korea's situation.
Crisis situations do not always provide only negative aspects. On the contrary, the difficulties brought about by mediocre product production will greatly highlight the need for innovation in Korean society as a whole to overcome this situation, and this will bring about the strengthening of innovation capabilities such as institutional reform and reform of the atmosphere for improved productivity and creative ideas in various fields such as politics, economy, society and culture.
In particular, there will be a strong need to reform the education system to foster creative talent, and it is expected that some visible results will be achieved. The variable that will have the greatest impact on these changes will be the ever-increasing number of overseas students, not only elementary, middle, and high school students, but also college students, who will contribute to the reform of Korea's education system. The article predicts that active voting by education consumers will drive change and innovation, and that politicians’ response to these demands will reshape Korean education.
If the reform of the education system that enables the training of creative talent succeeds and the innovation movement across society achieves results, there is still an opportunity to offset the decline in potential growth rate. The direction of institutional reform will also play an important role in determining Korea's shape over the next 10 years, and the choice of political leaders can be said to be decisive. Since the future is not just given but something to be created, it can be said that the selection of leaders relies heavily on the wisdom shown by Koreans.
Fourth, Korean companies are expected to gain momentum in expanding overseas, and a considerable number are expected to achieve outstanding results. Their efforts to enter overseas markets will spread beyond large corporations to small and midsize companies. Across both manufacturing and services, more companies that have proven themselves in the domestic market are expected to succeed as global players. Of all sectors of Korean society, Korean companies’ ability to survive and grow is the one I view most favorably.
Fifth, the remarkable growth of the financial industry will become another trend that will characterize the next 10 years. The Korean financial industry, which has played a role as an auxiliary to the manufacturing industry, is expected to achieve great growth thanks to institutional reforms such as the Capital Consolidation Act based on the bitter experience of the foreign exchange crisis, and some companies are expected to achieve great results in pioneering overseas markets. The growth of the financial industry means that the financial industry itself can occupy an important position in creating added value. In particular, the emergence of a financial industry that achieves outstanding results in the asset management field will greatly contribute to the creation of added value for investors. In any case, Korea's financial industry will be a case in which we can once again see how much success Koreans can achieve when given autonomy.
In addition to the conclusion of the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, the arena in which Koreans can operate will be greatly expanded as agreements with Europe, ASEAN, Japan, and China are partially concluded in the future. If the spirit of the times, such as autonomy, creativity, openness, and challenge, can once again occupy the center of Korean society, Koreans will be able to erase the sluggishness of the past and lay the foundation for a leap forward. We believe that the future is not given, but created by ourselves.
Source: Gong Byeong-ho Research Institute, Dr. Gong Byeong-ho, July 2007

ko-news-notices-376-8372c75064.title: Gore says ExxonMobil and other energy companies fund research disputing global warming
ko-news-notices-376-8372c75064.text:
Gore says ExxonMobil and other energy companies fund research disputing global warming
2022-03-02
Former U.S. Vice President Al Gore claimed on the 7th that large energy companies such as ExxonMobil are funding research that contradicts the scientific consensus on global warming in order to mislead the public.
ExxonMobil immediately issued a rebuttal statement.
At an environmental conference held in Singapore, former Vice President Gore criticized, "Some of the world's largest carbon-emitting companies have been disbursing $10 million a year in funds to systematically create the impression that there is controversy within the scientific community about warming."
He argued that warming is a topic on which the strongest consensus has been reached in the history of science, and that the move to overturn this is the same as the American tobacco companies investing large sums of money to create the impression that there is uncertainty and controversy within the scientific community regarding the harmful effects of smoking.
After the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change released a large-scale report last February warning that global warming is human-caused, former Vice President Gore criticized, saying, "Those who deny this offered a $10,000 incentive for each article that raised controversy in the UN report," and added, "They are trying to manipulate public opinion and treat us as fools."
He also emphasized that China, which will become the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter next year, should not be excluded from greenhouse gas reduction obligations because it is technically a developing country, and that China should skip technologies that pollute the environment and find ways to maintain growth.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for ExxonMobil said in a statement that the company's research funding was not intended to influence research, and that repeatedly raising groundless conspiracy theories was ignoring the realistic task of "how to supply the energy needed to improve living standards while reducing greenhouse gas emissions."
Last year, US and British scientists accused ExxonMobil of providing funding to groups that overturn the scientific consensus on climate change. (Singapore AP=Yonhap News)

Melting Arctic ice opens shorter routes between continents
2022-03-02
As global warming melts Arctic Ocean ice, shorter shipping routes between continents are becoming navigable.
The European Space Agency said satellite observations showed that melting Arctic sea ice off the coasts of Canada and Alaska had already made it possible for ships to travel through the Northwest Passage linking Europe and Asia.
Japan's Sankei Shimbun also reported that melting ice along Russia's Arctic coast had partially opened the Northeast Passage.
Sankei reported that once both routes were fully open, the sea route connecting Asia, Northern Europe, and the U.S. East Coast was expected to be about half as long as the current route.

ko-news-notices-380-8372c75064.title: Signs of abnormal water quality upstream of Saemangeum
ko-news-notices-380-8372c75064.text:
Signs of abnormal water quality upstream of Saemangeum
2022-03-02
‘Signs of abnormality’ in water quality upstream of Saemangeum
Despite the operation of the Jeonju Advanced Sewage Treatment Facility, the effect is minimal.
While Jeonbuk Province was pursuing various projects to improve water quality in the upper Saemangeum watershed, recent measurements in the Mangyeong River revealed signs of an anomaly. The findings put the province on high alert as it worked to identify the cause and prepare countermeasures.
Construction of the Jeonju advanced sewage-treatment facility, intended to fully treat wastewater flowing into the Mangyeong River, had been completed, and the facility was undergoing trial operation. Yet measurements indicated that water quality in the Mangyeong River had worsened, prompting calls for a detailed assessment of the system for protecting and managing Saemangeum’s water quality.
According to Jeonbuk Province on the 18th, a survey was conducted to assess the effect of the Jeonju advanced sewage-treatment facility, which had been in trial operation since the previous October, on improving water quality in the Mangyeong River, which is closely linked to Saemangeum’s water quality.
However, the survey produced data that provincial officials found difficult to explain, and they were divided over its cause.
After the advanced sewage-treatment facility began operating, BOD in the treatment plant’s effluent improved from 12 ppm before operation to 5.5 ppm afterward.
BOD in Jeonju Stream, into which the effluent flows, also fell from 9.0 ppm to 6.6 ppm, indicating that the advanced treatment facility was improving water quality.
Yet in the Mangyeong River near Samnye, Wanju County, where the improved water from Jeonju Stream flows in, measured BOD rose from 5.0 ppm to 6.0 ppm.
Even within the province, opinions differed over these water-quality results, which seemed counterintuitive.
Some believed that a factor might be degrading water quality between the point where Jeonju Stream joins the Mangyeong River and the measurement site. Others viewed the increase as a temporary phenomenon caused by the fact that none of the seven water-quality improvement projects then under way in the upper Saemangeum watershed had been completed. The projects included 26 advanced sewage-treatment facilities (4 completed and 22 not yet completed), sewer-network works, a privately funded reinforcement project for the Wanggung livestock-wastewater treatment facility, management of livestock manure from individual farms, improvement of natural streams, and ongoing efforts to reduce nonpoint-source pollution through eco-friendly agriculture.
The province planned to ask experts from the Environmental Countermeasures Committee under the Office for Government Policy Coordination to conduct a field investigation the following month, identify the precise cause of these findings, and devise countermeasures.
Reporter Nam Hyeong-jin

Next year’s tide predictions for Korea’s coast announced
2022-03-02
Next year’s tide predictions for Korea’s coast announced
National Oceanographic Research Institute forecasts tides at 52 coastal locations
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (Director Yeon Young-jin) announced its predictions of high- and low-tide times and heights for 2008 at 52 coastal locations, including major ports such as Busan, Incheon, and Mokpo, as well as the Ieodo Ocean Research Station.
According to the agency, particularly high tide levels were expected in July, August, and September next year. The year’s highest tides were forecast for around July 3–5 (lunar June 1–3) and August 1–3 (lunar July 1–3).
The forecast peak tide heights for major locations were: west coast—Incheon, 935 cm (August 3 and October 16); Pyeongtaek, 947 cm (August 3); Gunsan Outer Harbor, 736 cm (August 3); and Mokpo, 512 cm (July 4); south coast—Busan, 146 cm (August 1 and 2); Masan, 223 cm (August 2); Jeju, 294 cm (July 3); and Ieodo, 290 cm (June 4).
The predicted peak tide height could vary considerably with weather conditions such as wind and atmospheric pressure. Sea levels could also rise sharply during July–September, when typhoons and other severe weather often occur, so particular caution was advised in low-lying areas.
Next year’s forecast adds four newly established tidal stations—Janghang, Jindo, Goheung, and Geoje Island—to the 47 locations covered in previous years, along with the Ieodo station, which had been managed and operated since 2007.
The forecast results were to be published in the Korea Coastal Tide Tables issued by the agency and sold at chart and nautical-publication outlets nationwide from early September (inquiries: 02-701-9981). They would also be available on the agency’s website (www.nori.go.kr).

NORI dispatches expert to help developing countries prevent marine disasters

The dispatch was carried out in cooperation with the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) as part of Korea’s grant-based official development assistance (ODA) to support recovery from tsunami damage caused by the earthquake that struck Sumatra, Indonesia, in December 2004. During the three-month assignment, the expert planned to transfer marine-observation technology and knowledge for establishing a tsunami-forecasting system, helping Indonesia build its capacity to minimize marine-related disasters.
The support was expected to provide a good opportunity to strengthen ties with Indonesia, a full member of the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) and the East Asian Hydrographic Commission (EAHC), and to enhance Korea’s standing in the international community.
An agency official said, “The waters around the Strait of Malacca near Indonesia are an important international shipping route used by Korean vessels. This dispatch offers two benefits: building Indonesia’s marine-technology capacity and surveying conditions along major shipping lanes.”

ko-news-notices-383-8372c75064.title: Hydrographic surveys completed at major East Coast ports
ko-news-notices-383-8372c75064.text:
Hydrographic surveys completed at major East Coast ports

The National Oceanographic Research Institute’s East Sea Oceanographic Survey Office (Director Kim Jeong-gi) announced that it had completed hydrographic surveys of Donghae, Samcheok, and Ulsan (Mipo) ports, which began in April.
These are major East Coast ports with frequent large-vessel traffic, where up-to-date seafloor topographic data are needed.
The survey found no major change in the depth distribution at Donghae Port. Depths near Chuam ranged from 24 to 27 m, but an area with a shallow depth of 18 m was found where artificial reefs had been placed. The survey also found that dredging had increased the depth of a 4.6 m shoal near the southern entrance to and exit from Ulsan (Mipo) Port to 9.1 m.
An official from the National Oceanographic Research Institute said, “We expect to update nautical charts promptly with the survey results and provide current information that will help ensure maritime traffic safety and serve as baseline data for port management and operation and marine development.”

ko-news-notices-384-8372c75064.title: Han River estuary: begin with a joint North–South survey
ko-news-notices-384-8372c75064.text:
Han River estuary: begin with a joint North–South survey
2022-03-02
The inter-Korean summit had raised the prospect of developing the Han River basin. The Grand National Party and the United New Democratic Party had also announced development of the Han River estuary and a grand canal project as campaign pledges. Lee Myung-bak, then a presidential candidate, pledged to build an artificial island of about 29.75 million square meters (9 million pyeong) northeast of Gyodong Island in Ganghwa County, at the mouth of the Han River. Lee Hae-chan, then a candidate in the party primary, pledged that dredging the sand deposited where the Han and Imjin rivers meet and using it as construction material would prevent recurrent flooding and reduce logistics costs by creating a canal between Gaeseong and Paldang.
However, the two candidates know too little about the Han River. The tidal range at its estuary is about 10 meters. One sees only the flooding at high tide; the other, only the tidal flats exposed at low tide.
The Han River basin covers 38,665 square kilometers. Rainwater falling across an area equal to 17.4% of the Korean Peninsula flows into the Namhan, Bukhan, Imjin, and Yeseong rivers, which meet at the estuary; 70% of the water is discharged during the flood season. Water is a resource nearly as valuable as oil. Building a dike across the estuary to create a freshwater lake could secure vast quantities of industrial water, make use of extensive tidal flats and high-quality sediment, and prevent estuary flooding. An artificial island, however, would cause flooding.
The Han River estuary’s potential lies in its capacity to become a new economic hub in Northeast Asia. Tokyo in Japan in the 1960s, Seoul in the 1970s, the Pearl River estuary special economic zone in China in the 1980s, Shanghai’s Pudong at the Yangtze River estuary in the 1990s, and the Yellow River estuary and Bohai Bay in the 2000s were successive growth centers. In the 2010s, the Korean Peninsula should become a growth hub for Northeast Asia. The key to developing the Han River estuary is not narrow measures such as flood prevention, river aggregate extraction, or artificial islands; it is how to maximize the estuary’s potential and make it a Northeast Asian growth hub.
Building a dike across the Han River estuary would make it possible to use abundant water resources and extensive tidal flats to develop a peace-oriented industrial complex, a free-trade zone, new cities, and a major hub port needed for industrialization on a reunified Korean Peninsula. It is important to develop the estuary’s potential through inter-Korean economic cooperation that can compete with Japan and China. Above all, the two Koreas must work together to assess the economic feasibility of the Han River estuary, reach agreement, and establish a new economic system. Instead of rushing into development projects, they should begin with a joint study of the estuary’s potential and the need for development.
Source: JoongAng Ilbo, October 10, 2007
Kim Gwang-nam, President, Construction Business Management Research Institute

ko-news-notices-385-8372c75064.title: Saemangeum reclaimed land could generate economic benefits on the scale of Dubai’s oil wealth
ko-news-notices-385-8372c75064.text:
Saemangeum reclaimed land could generate economic benefits on the scale of Dubai’s oil wealth
2022-03-02
“Rumble, rumble, thud.”
That is the sound of excavators placing rocks to build a seawall at the Saemangeum construction site, which is changing Korea’s map.
The final closure works were completed on April 21 of the previous year, and seawall construction is now in full swing. The seawall links Daehang-ri in Byeonsan-myeon, Buan County, North Jeolla Province, with Bieungdo Island in Gunsan.
At the Saemangeum Exhibition Hall in Daehang-ri, its director, Park Deok-yeol, explained: “The seawall is divided into four sections: Section 1, Daehang-ri to the Garyeok sluice gate (4.7 km); Section 2, the Garyeok sluice gate to the Sinsi sluice gate (9.9 km); Section 3, the Sinsi sluice gate to Yami-do (2.7 km); and Section 4, Yami-do to Bieungdo (11.4 km).”
The Saemangeum seawall is 1 km longer than the Netherlands’ Zuiderzee dike, previously considered the world’s longest at 32 km.
The four sections of the seawall total 28.7 km, shorter than the Zuiderzee dike. But adding the two sluice gates, which together span 660 m, and the 3 km Bieungdo section being built by Gunsan City brings the total length above that of the Zuiderzee dike.
At present, only Section 1 (4.7 km), completed by Daewoo Engineering & Construction, and the Garyeok sluice gate are open to visitors. The Sinsi sluice gate, already completed, and Sections 2, 3, and 4, which are still under construction, were not expected to open to the public until the end of 2009.
Director Park accompanied the reporter through the restricted area from Section 2 to Bieungdo.
Except for Section 1, work on the outer and inner seawalls was proceeding simultaneously along the entire Saemangeum seawall. At several points along the inner seawall, black, muddy water gushed from large steel pipes.
Park explained: “Saemangeum is being reclaimed with sediment dredged from the sea. A dredger pumps the material from the sea outside the seawall through a large pipe. At the other end, inside the seawall, water mixed with the dredged sediment flows out. The water is drained away, and only the sand and soil are used to build the seawall and fill the reclaimed land.”
Building the seawall alone required enough earth and sand to fill 14.3 million 15-ton dump trucks. That volume would be enough to build the 416 km Gyeongbu Expressway from Seoul to Busan to a height of 7 m.
The project team was circulating seawater through the reclaimed area and regularly draining water through 18 Garyeok and Sinsi sluice bays (36 gates). Each gate was 30 m wide, 15 m high, and weighed 484 tons. The Sinsi sluice released 8,812 tons of water per second, and the Garyeok sluice 7,050 tons per second.
Once the drainage work was completed, the Saemangeum reclaimed area—40,100 ha in total, comprising 28,300 ha of land and an 11,800 ha freshwater lake—was expected to be created by 2011. That area is equivalent to 66% of Seoul’s area, and development was planned in phases through 2030.
According to Park, after the land was formed, development in the Dongjin River area, where water quality was relatively good, was planned for completion by 2020. In the Mangyeong River area, seawater circulation would be maintained until water-quality standards were met, with development to be completed by 2030.
The reclamation project was guided by a principle of environmentally friendly development. Farmland, considered more environmentally friendly than other types of industrial land use, accounted for 56.9% of the total land area. Only 6.6% was allocated to industrial complexes, an area Park said would exceed domestic industrial demand.
Park said: “This reclaimed land gives top priority to environmental sustainability. Unlike Lake Sihwa, which is known as a failed reclamation project, we have put comprehensive environmental measures in place. We will continue to address any shortcomings and develop further measures.”
Water quality in Saemangeum was being managed in three areas: the Dongjin and Mangyeong River basins, the freshwater lake within the reclaimed area, and the seawater outside the seawall.
As Park said, the land and water resources could generate economic benefits comparable to Dubai’s oil resources. It seemed that before long the Saemangeum reclaimed land would become fertile ground for creating a “new Mangeum” (“ten thousand gold”) in the 21st century.
The Gogunsan Islands, viewed from the Sinsi sluice gate.
Saemangeum is being reclaimed with sediment dredged from the sea. A dredger pumps the material from the sea outside the seawall through a large pipe. At the other end, inside the seawall, water mixed with the dredged sediment flows out. The water is drained away, and only the sand and soil are used to build the seawall and fill the reclaimed land. The photo shows the Section 2 seawall construction site, where Hyundai Engineering & Construction was carrying out the work.
Reporter Su-nam Jeong perec@asiatoday.co.kr

ko-news-notices-386-8372c75064.title: If you want to be good at internal politics...
ko-news-notices-386-8372c75064.text:
If you want to be good at internal politics...
2022-03-02
If you want to be good at internal politics...
Even if you feel disgusted by the behavior of established politicians, you cannot get rid of politics. Whether you like office politics or not, you cannot deny its existence. The mainstream view is that office politics is also a part of competitiveness. The secrets to success in corporate politics revealed in management books and the writings of successful CEOs are very diverse. However, if you group them into large categories, they can be divided into 5 categories.
1. Build your skills before speaking
If you are a new employee who has been with the company for less than 5 years, it is better to completely forget about office politics. If you make unnecessary efforts to cultivate connections with people here and there, you may only become the subject of gossip. Even if you think you're smart, everyone's lives are similar. In particular, there are many cases where a junior's political maneuvering is clearly visible to seniors or department superiors. Mr. Lee (32), an employee at a local company, does not miss out on drinking parties with his seniors. He reported all the personnel and new-policy information he picked up to his direct supervisor. Before moving to another department, the supervisor, who had always been fond of him, called Lee in and said: “I’ve heard a lot of comments like, ‘If you’re always out drinking, when do you get any work done?’ It’s good to spend time with senior and junior colleagues and build relationships, but first make sure you handle your own work. And from now on, I may not feel I can speak freely when we drink together.”
2. Don’t try to beat your boss.
You can never succeed by turning your back on your boss. To be good at company politics, you need to develop followership, a concept that corresponds to leadership. A follower is different from a yes man or sycophant. It literally means ‘right-hand man’ who assists and keeps the boss in check. Conflict may arise. If the direction of work is different, try to understand your boss's position before criticizing him or her for being ignorant or just selfish. 'Words' can easily lead to misunderstanding depending on the nuance. It is also a good idea to write down work progress, opinions, complaints, etc. by e-mail.
3. Learn how to communicate
It's easy to criticize anyone, but it is difficult to offer pointed, sincere praise. Look at a project proposal presented by a colleague or rival and do not hesitate to praise the parts that you can truly learn from. After listening sufficiently, offer your views constructively. Anyone can criticize something by saying something cannot be done, and it can make oneself look like a complainer. Even when reporting to your superiors, you must clearly understand your tendencies. Give an impatient boss the key points right away; give a boss who provides only broad direction a detailed account of any areas that may need attention.
4. Have a future-oriented mindset.
How do you present alternatives to your boss? There are types who list several alternatives, explain the pros and cons, and then leave the decision to their superiors, and there are types who come up with what they think is the best policy and convince them of the reasons. Usually, bosses like the latter. This is because it gives the impression that the junior is working on this policy with insight and responsibility. In other words, in order to succeed within the company, you must approach each task as if you were the one doing it yourself, that is, with a ‘manager’s mindset’ rather than an ‘office worker’s mindset’. At the same time, you need to reveal the dreams you want to achieve within the company whenever you have the opportunity. When there is a personnel change, superiors naturally think, 'That person would be good for that job.'
5. Mentor junior colleagues
Gil-seon Cho, a business consultant and author of '10 Survival Skills', said, "I have lived with the thought that 15% of my salary is not mine." He gave it to his juniors who needed financial help without hesitation. Those colleagues are likely to become loyal members of his circle. Even in the era of self-PR, it is shameful to talk about one's own achievements. At times like this, junior colleagues can become “praise trumpeters.” Though they may be newcomers now, they can provide crucial support when you later seek to establish yourself as a team leader or department head.
Reporter Kim Soo-yong ksy@msnet.co.kr

ko-news-notices-387-8372c75064.title: Shim Dong-hyun takes office as director of the National Oceanographic Research Institute
ko-news-notices-387-8372c75064.text:
Shim Dong-hyun takes office as director of the National Oceanographic Research Institute
2022-03-02
Shim Dong-hyun takes office as director of the National Oceanographic Research Institute
Shim Dong-hyun, 50, took office on the 5th as the 31st director of the National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI).
In his inaugural address, Shim said the institute would improve the efficiency of its work and take an active part in international activities that produce information to international standards, thereby strengthening its global competitiveness.
Shim began his civil-service career as an administrative officer in 1983. He has held a range of key posts, including chief of general affairs at the Yeosu Regional Maritime and Port Office, an assignment to the Seattle Port Authority in the United States, chief of the Port Operations Improvement Division in the Bureau of Shipping and Logistics, and chief of the Marine Environment Division in the Marine Policy Bureau. Most recently, he was seconded to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). He is a career maritime and fisheries official.
Shim graduated from Jeonju High School and Seoul National University, where he also earned a master’s degree in law.
He and his wife, Joo Hyeon-hee, have one son and one daughter.

ko-news-notices-388-8372c75064.title: Unmanned submersible Haemirae begins its first exploration in the Ulleung Basin of the East Sea
ko-news-notices-388-8372c75064.text:
Unmanned submersible Haemirae begins its first exploration in the Ulleung Basin of the East Sea
2022-03-02
Unmanned submersible Haemirae begins its first exploration in the Ulleung Basin of the East Sea
Three marine-animal rescue and rehabilitation centers designated; treatment of injured animals to begin in earnest
Haemirae, a 6,000-meter-class unmanned underwater vehicle developed by Korea as the world’s fourth country to do so, after the United States, Japan, and France, is to begin its first exploration in the Ulleung Basin of the East Sea.
At a regular briefing on the morning of the 8th, Shin Pyeong-sik, head of the Marine Policy Headquarters at the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries (MOMAF), said: “After completing several performance tests, the unmanned underwater vehicle Haemirae has been conducting full-scale seabed exploration at a depth of 1,500 m in the Ulleung Basin of the East Sea from the 1st through the 12th of this month.”
Conceptual diagram of Haemirae’s exploration
Carried aboard the oceanographic research vessel Onnuri, Haemirae will be operated by a 26-member exploration team, including Dr. Pan-muk Lee of the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute (KORDI). The team will observe the Ulleung Basin’s ecological environment, collect seafloor samples, and conduct detailed surveys of seafloor topography.
The unmanned underwater vehicle Haemirae has a total mass of 3,700 kg and is equipped with a robotic arm, various measuring instruments, underwater cameras, and lighting.
In particular, six electric thrusters allow Haemirae to move forward and backward, left and right, and up and down at 1.0–1.5 knots. It is also equipped with an ultra-short baseline (USBL) positioning system that can track a target with an error of ±5 m.
From 2001 through last year, MOMAF and KORDI invested 12 billion won to develop Haemirae and its launch-and-recovery system, Haenubi. Performance testing and operational-software tests had been completed in the East Sea and the Pacific.
Haemirae is expected to be used to explore cold seeps and hydrothermal vents in the East Sea and Pacific, investigate subsea resources such as methane hydrate, and support research on marine ecosystems and new materials.
MOMAF also designated three specialized rescue and rehabilitation centers for marine animals—the Seoul Grand Park, Haeundae Aquarium in Busan, and Pacific Land in Jeju—to treat injured or stranded animals and return them to the wild.
Although the number of marine animals injured or stranded because of human activities has been increasing each year, no national-level rescue and rehabilitation centers had existed, making it difficult to treat animals even when live ones were found.
Species expected to be covered include minke whales, common dolphins, finless porpoises, Pacific white-sided dolphins, harbor porpoises, Risso’s dolphins, false killer whales, bottlenose dolphins, spotted seals, fur seals, Steller sea lions, otters, loggerhead sea turtles, and green sea turtles.
MOMAF estimated that about 24 cetaceans and 1–6 sea turtles were caught as bycatch or stranded along Korea’s coasts each year.
The ministry also anticipated that the perceived economic value of marine animals might discourage people from reporting them. To encourage reports and make rescue efforts more effective, it said it would consider paying rewards to people who report live marine animals or help with their rescue and treatment.

ko-news-notices-389-8372c75064.title: Marine science and technology will shape our future in the 21st century
ko-news-notices-389-8372c75064.text:
Marine science and technology will shape our future in the 21st century
2022-03-02
Marine science and technology will shape our future in the 21st century
Column in the Rotary section of Seoul Economic Daily (November 8)
“2013: Aboard the research vessel Onnuri in the Clarion–Clipperton Zone of the deep Pacific, about 2,000 km southeast of Hawaii. Researchers are hard at work testing a mining system to harvest manganese nodules from Korea’s exclusive exploration area, 5,000 m below the seafloor. A few minutes later, the system begins continuously bringing up potato-shaped black nodules. The researchers, drenched with sweat, break into broad smiles.
A few years later, after the technology has been transferred to a private company and commercial development of the nodules has begun, it will be possible to mine 3 million tons of manganese nodules each year for about 100 years. The nodules contain key strategic metals such as copper, nickel, and cobalt. Imagining that future, the researchers are moved by the thought that their years of work are finally bearing fruit.”
This is the scene that comes to mind and makes me smile whenever I think about marine science and technology.
The research vessel Onnuri
The ocean is emerging as a storehouse of future resources that can replace dwindling land-based resources and as a means of human survival that can help address climate change caused by global warming. Marine science and technology is a future-oriented field that can help solve shared challenges facing humanity in the 21st century and secure sustainable drivers of national growth by developing the ocean. Advanced countries around the world are making every effort to gain leadership in the marine sector by developing marine science and technology.
Since the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries (MOMAF) was established in 1996, Korea has increased its investment in marine science and technology. This has produced visible results, including construction of the Ieodo Ocean Research Station and development of the world’s fourth 6,000-meter-class deep-sea unmanned underwater vehicle. Korea has laid the groundwork for new marine industries through deep-ocean water, construction of the world’s largest tidal power plant at Lake Sihwa, and marine biotechnology. It has also secured a 40,000-square-kilometer manganese-nodule exploration area in the international waters of the Pacific, with annual production of strategic metal resources valued at 2 trillion won anticipated. Development of an icebreaker for polar exploration and a second Antarctic station is also proceeding steadily.
View of Ieodo
“Wanting to understand the sea is not a matter of simple curiosity; our survival depends on it.”
These were words U.S. President John F. Kennedy delivered to Congress in 1961 as he emphasized the need to develop the oceans. The time has come to strengthen efforts to develop marine science and technology as a clear blue-ocean strategy for preparing for our future and survival.
Kang Moo-hyun, Minister of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries

ko-news-notices-390-8372c75064.title: ‘Encouragement’ and ‘praise’ help people grow
ko-news-notices-390-8372c75064.text:
‘Encouragement’ and ‘praise’ help people grow
2022-03-02
‘Encouragement’ and ‘praise’ help people grow
A Korean proverb says, “A single word can repay even a thousand-nyang debt.” Another says, “Praise can make even a whale dance.” The point is that a few words can give someone courage and even move their heart. In business, material rewards are of course important for motivating employees, but warm words of encouragement and praise often do much to boost morale.
3M, widely known as a leading example of an innovative company, is also known for a management philosophy that emphasizes praise and encouragement to help employees show initiative and creativity. William L. McKnight, 3M’s legendary early CEO, applauded employees who pursued innovation. He believed, “Managers who harshly criticize employees for making mistakes are killing their initiative. People who take initiative are essential to our continued growth.” He was generous in encouraging employees when their efforts failed. The distinctive management philosophy of successive leaders helped make 3M the world-class company it is today.
Psychological rewards make their recipients happy, regardless of their size. Used well, encouragement and praise can sometimes be more effective than material rewards. Managers should not automatically reprimand subordinates for mistakes. Rewards and penalties should of course be clear; at the same time, managers should respond in proportion to the seriousness of each case, recognize subordinates’ strengths, and offer praise and encouragement where appropriate. This can nurture employees’ latent creativity and spur voluntary innovation. Companies need to reaffirm that people are ultimately the source of their competitiveness and consider effective ways to motivate them.
Source: Hyundai Research Institute, Chairperson’s Note No. 173

ko-news-notices-391-8372c75064.title: Portable Charts and Maritime Traffic Maps to Be Produced and Distributed Free of Charge
ko-news-notices-391-8372c75064.text:
Portable Charts and Maritime Traffic Maps to Be Produced and Distributed Free of Charge
2022-03-02
Portable charts and maritime traffic maps to be produced and distributed free of charge
Portable marine thematic charts designed for easy carrying; expected to serve the general public and maritime and fisheries professionals
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director Shim Dong-hyeon) announced that it would produce portable charts and maritime traffic information maps for ports with heavy vessel traffic, including New Port and Mokpo Port, and begin distributing them free of charge in mid-January.
The portable charts are folded to A3 size for easy carrying and cover New Port, Sokcho, Daesan, Jeju, and Mokpo Port. Their front sides show key information such as tide forecasts, port regulations, emergency contact numbers, and coastal mileage tables; the corresponding nautical chart appears on the reverse.
The maritime traffic information maps for Masan, Yeosu, Gunsan, and Mokpo ports include precautions for entering and leaving port, information about the vessel traffic service (VTS), and information on Korea’s Marine Pollution Prevention Act.
An agency official said, “We expect that distributing these portable charts and maritime traffic information maps will make key port information easy for mariners and maritime and fisheries professionals to carry and use. We also plan to produce and distribute a range of marine thematic charts to make them more convenient for users.”
The portable charts and maritime traffic information maps will be distributed free of charge to mariners and maritime and fisheries organizations, including pilot associations and shipping companies. For information, contact the Chart Division at 032-885-3825.

ko-news-notices-392-8372c75064.text:
Bottled Deep Sea Water May Be Launched This Year
2022-03-02
Bottled deep sea water may be launched this year
Enforcement Decree and Enforcement Rule promulgated on February 4, completing the framework for full-scale business development
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries announced that the Enforcement Decree and Enforcement Rule for the Development and Management of Deep Sea Water Act, enacted on August 3 of the previous year, had been promulgated and that the Act would take full effect on February 4.
The main provisions established by the subordinate regulations include rates for fees and charges for using deep sea water; the depth at which it may be taken; water-quality standards; detailed criteria for licensing reviews; and facility standards for deep sea water development businesses.
After beginning work on this legislation in February 2004, the ministry has completed the institutional framework four years later. The law aims to create a new marine industry and contribute to the public’s healthy lives by developing and using deep sea water, a resource of the future.
With the Act taking full effect, deep sea water is expected to be used in many fields, from producing beverages, alcoholic drinks, cosmetics, and medicines to developing aquaculture for cold-water species and health-and-leisure industries such as spas. Related industries forecast that the deep sea water market will reach the KRW 1 trillion range annually within the next five years.
The ministry plans to receive applications for designation of sea water intake areas from the relevant mayors and county heads by the end of this month, designate the areas after review by the Deep Sea Water Committee, and promptly complete the administrative procedures needed to issue deep sea water development business licenses by June.

ko-news-notices-393-8372c75064.title: Long-Term Plan to Restore the Taean Ecosystem After the Oil Spill
ko-news-notices-393-8372c75064.text:
Long-Term Plan to Restore the Taean Ecosystem After the Oil Spill
2022-03-02
Long-term plan to restore the Taean ecosystem after the oil spill
Domestic and international oil-pollution experts, including NOAA, begin an on-site impact survey
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries has urgently formed a task force of domestic and international oil-pollution experts to scientifically assess damage to the marine and coastal environment from the oil spill that occurred off Mallipo in Taean County on the 7th. The task force will conduct an environmental impact survey and prepare a long-term ecosystem-restoration plan.
The domestic task force, assembled with the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute at its center, plans to begin field investigations as soon as possible and work closely with three oil-spill response specialists from the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) and one marine-ecosystem specialist from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), who arrived in Korea on the 13th. Eight more experts were expected to arrive on the 15th from the European Union (EU), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), and other organizations. They specialize in oil-spill crisis management, assessment of pollution conditions, emergency spill response, and medium- and long-term environmental impact assessment. Together, the experts will investigate the environmental effects of the Taean spill and prepare a long-term ecosystem-restoration plan.
Under the Marine Environment Management Act, when 100 kL or more of pollutants are discharged from a vessel into the sea, the owner of the vessel or marine facility must have a marine-pollution impact survey conducted through an authorized survey agency within three months of the incident. In this case, however, the discharge greatly exceeded that threshold and the spreading pollutants were causing extensive damage to aquaculture facilities. Under the relevant exception provisions, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries therefore took the lead in urgently conducting an assessment of the pollution’s impact on the marine environment.
After the 1995 Sea Prince oil spill, the failure to collect scientific evidence and make observations promptly for an initial impact assessment made it difficult to prove economic losses to the International Oil Pollution Compensation Funds (IOPC Funds). Drawing on that experience and the current spill’s severity, the ministry convened domestic experts for a response meeting as an emergency measure in the Hebei Spirit incident.
The results of the on-site oil-spill impact survey, to be conducted shortly with ministry support, will provide a scientific assessment of the actual environmental effects and economic losses in Taean waters. They will be used in claims for compensation from the IOPC Funds and will provide baseline information for developing and implementing a long-term ecosystem-restoration plan. This prompt response is significant not only because it initiates a scientific assessment of pollution impacts, but also because it signals the ministry’s commitment to long-term restoration of the marine and coastal ecosystems affected by the spill.

ko-news-notices-394-8372c75064.title: Korea Marine Environment Management Corporation Launched
ko-news-notices-394-8372c75064.text:
Korea Marine Environment Management Corporation Launched
2022-03-02
Korea Marine Environment Management Corporation launched to manage the marine environment comprehensively
Expanded functions of the Korea Marine Pollution Response Corporation; launch scheduled for the 21st
The Korea Marine Pollution Response Corporation, established in November 1997 as part of the response measures following the Sea Prince accident in July 1995, will be relaunched as the Korea Marine Environment Management Corporation after 11 years.
The Korea Marine Environment Management Corporation was established under Article 96 of the Marine Environment Management Act, which took effect on January 20, 2008. With the vision of becoming “a specialized agency for the integrated management of Korea’s marine environment,” the corporation’s establishment committee—chaired by the Vice Minister of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries—has been preparing for its launch since April 2007.
The expanded corporation will carry out projects to conserve, manage, and improve the marine environment; respond to marine pollution; and develop technology and provide education and training related to the marine environment and pollution. By streamlining the Korea Marine Pollution Response Corporation’s operations, the expansion adds only five positions, bringing the authorized staffing complement to 485: three headquarters, two offices, one center, 17 teams, and 12 regional branches nationwide.
Because most employees have been deployed to the Hebei Spirit spill site and must focus on shoreline response, the corporation decided to forgo a large launch ceremony and hold only a brief signboard-unveiling ceremony at its office in Samseong-dong, Gangnam-gu, Seoul, on the 21st.
An official from the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries said, “As Korea’s only specialized organization for marine-environment conservation, the corporation will faithfully carry out professional and efficient spill-response work—work that is difficult for the government, local governments, and the private sector to perform—and become an organization trusted by the public.”

ko-news-notices-395-8372c75064.text:
Regulations on Hydrographic Survey Operations Revised
2022-03-02
Regulations on hydrographic survey operations revised
Helping local governments resolve maritime-boundary disputes
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI; Director Shim Dong-hyeon) announced on the 17th that it had revised the Regulations on Hydrographic Survey Operations. The revised rules cover surveys to delineate maritime boundaries and the use of airborne laser surveying, an advanced survey technique.
Recent port development has heightened local governments’ interest in maritime boundaries and led to continuing disputes over jurisdictional authority and permits for marine sand extraction. Surveys of exposed rocks on islands and offshore have also been required to use airborne laser technology because those sites are difficult to access and conventional surveys take considerable time.
Under the revised rules, disputes over maritime-boundary delineation are addressed by using the coastline as a reference and the median line as the boundary; GPS surveys are to provide precise location data. The rules also provide for airborne laser surveys to map inundation-prone areas and navigational hazards in a short time, thereby improving efficiency.
To ensure reliable marine information and accurate data, the institute also specified that qualified experts collect data using modern equipment and that the Korea Hydrographic Survey Association, with extensive field experience, review it.
An institute official said, “These revised hydrographic survey regulations establish a basis for user-oriented services by clarifying the location and facts of maritime-boundary dispute areas and setting out the use of the new airborne laser surveying method.”

ko-news-notices-396-8372c75064.title: An Era of Ubiquitous Mobile Connectivity at Sea Is Dawning
ko-news-notices-396-8372c75064.text:
An Era of Ubiquitous Mobile Connectivity at Sea Is Dawning
2022-03-02
The Ubiquitous Mobile-Phone Era at Sea Is Dawning
Safety information network for people at sea to be built by installing mobile-phone repeaters at lighthouses
The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries announced on the 6th that it plans to install mobile-phone repeaters at lighthouse facilities and build a ubiquitous safety information network, helping people enjoy safer activities at sea wherever they are as the number of people using small fishing vessels, angling boats, and recreational boats increases.
The ministry’s Safety Management Office, headed by Director Jeon Byeong-jo, said it would install repeaters at lighthouses along the nation’s coasts to improve safety and convenience for people at sea without a large budget, making mobile calls possible in waters around the lighthouses. In consultation with mobile carriers including KTF, LG Telecom, and SK Telecom, it also plans to install the repeaters and develop waterproof mobile phones.
System configuration diagram
A ministry official said that on the western and southern coasts, where there are many islands, large tidal ranges, and strong currents, reliable mobile reception in bad sea weather would alert boaters to a nearby lighthouse equipped with a repeater. This could encourage safer navigation by small fishing vessels, angling boats, and recreational boats and help prevent accidents.
Anyone who wishes to do so will also be able to obtain real-time marine-weather and route information from a staffed lighthouse. If someone at sea needs emergency medical care or is in danger, they can use a staffed lighthouse to request prompt medical evacuation or rescue from the Korea Coast Guard.
Plan to expand mobile coverage
The ministry plans to work with mobile carriers including KTF, LG Telecom, and SK Telecom to install repeaters at lighthouse facilities and actively advance the project starting this year. It aims to establish a rapid-response system for accidents and distress at sea, contributing to maritime-traffic safety and marine-environment conservation and improving the safety of people at sea.
A ministry official said the measure was prompted by the need for people at sea to have a way to communicate quickly from ship to ship and from ship to shore.
In May 2005, a recreational boat was stranded for 14 hours near Ipado Island off the west coast, and all seven members of one family died. The official said lives might have been saved if they had been able to make a phone call.
When a maritime accident, medical emergency, or other danger occurs, people need access to a communication method that is easy to use and can quickly get a message through.
For now, mobile phones—the means of communication most people can readily use—are the only such option. However, calls are possible only within about 20 km of the mainland or islands, and reception is poor farther out at sea. The ministry said this measure was devised to help ensure safety at sea.

Woo Ye-jong Takes Office as Director General of the National Oceanographic Research Institute
2022-03-02
Woo Ye-jong takes office as Director General of the National Oceanographic Research Institute
On March 21, Woo Ye-jong, 48, took office as the 32nd Director General of the National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI).
Woo graduated from Dankook University and passed the 28th Higher Civil Service Examination. He began his public-service career in 1985 as an administrative officer in the Port Affairs Bureau of the Korea Maritime and Port Administration. He later held key posts including Head of the Resource Management Division in the Fisheries Resources Bureau of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, Head of the International Cooperation Division, and Planning and Budget Officer. He also served as Deputy Head of the Northeast Asian Logistics Hub Planning Group and was assigned to the Korea National Defense University for national-security studies. He was appointed Director General of NORI under the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs.
In his inaugural address, Woo said, “I will work to improve the efficiency of our agency’s operations and actively take part in international activities that produce information at the international level, thereby strengthening our global competitiveness.”
He also said, “At a time when international attention to global warming is growing and hydrographic surveys and ocean observations are becoming increasingly important for responding to abnormal weather, typhoons, earthquakes, and other natural disasters, I will do my utmost to ensure that the National Oceanographic Research Institute helps lay the groundwork for building a leading nation through the ocean.”

ko-news-notices-399-8372c75064.title: Sea Fog Peaks in May; Collision-Accident Warning Issued
ko-news-notices-399-8372c75064.text:
Sea Fog Peaks in May; Collision-Accident Warning Issued
2022-03-02
Sea fog peaks in May; collision-accident warning issued
Shipping companies urged to sail safely, including by adjusting schedules
According to the Central Maritime Safety Tribunal’s May 2008 Marine Safety Outlook, maritime fog was the leading accident risk in May. The tribunal called for crew training to prevent accidents during the fog season.
Over the past five years, marine accidents in May were recorded in the following order: collisions, 63 cases (28.5%); engine damage, 53 (24.0%); groundings, 21 (9.5%); fires and explosions, 20 (9.0%); casualties, 14 (6.3%); distress and sinking, 8 (3.7%); and other accidents, 34 (15.3%).
Fog-related collisions often occur because a vessel detects an approaching ship too late and the collision happens while it is taking evasive action. They tend to cause major vessel damage and loss of life.
The Golden Rose incident, which caused public outrage over a suspected hit-and-run at sea and the loss of 16 lives, also occurred in May of the previous year.
Vessels passing through fog should reduce speed to a safe level, keep a careful radar lookout, and sound fog signals. If there is a risk of collision, they should slow to the minimum speed at which they can maintain their course.
A tribunal official said, “During the fog season, crews must be retrained in the rules for navigating in restricted visibility. It would also help prevent accidents if shipping companies planned schedules with enough leeway to keep captains from being pressured into unsafe operations.” The tribunal urged shipping companies to operate safely.
The outlook also found that safety management needed to be strengthened for water-recreation boats, excursion and ferry vessels, and fishing boats, where the concentration of holidaymakers in May raises accident risks.

ko-news-notices-400-8372c75064.text:
Integrated Management of Marine Environmental Surveys Begins
2022-03-02
Integrated management of marine environmental surveys begins
Ministry launches comprehensive marine-ecosystem survey in the Jeonnam region
An integrated environmental-management system is expected to be established at sea as well.
The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs announced that it would hold a kickoff briefing for the 2008 Comprehensive Marine Ecosystem Survey at Mokpo City Hall in Jeollanam-do on April 30.
About 20 specialist organizations are participating, including government agencies such as the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs, the National Institute of Fisheries Science, and the Tidal Flat Research Center, as well as the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute, universities, environmental businesses and organizations, and NGOs. The comprehensive survey brings the survey areas of several projects conducted by the ministry under a unified plan. It focuses on the Jeonnam region to maximize policy impact by combining three projects that had been carried out separately since 2006: the Basic Marine Ecosystem Survey, the Coastal Wetlands Baseline Survey, and research to establish an estuary-management system.
About 200 local government officials, residents, and related experts are expected to attend the kickoff briefing. The agenda will begin with an introduction to the ministry’s marine-ecosystem conservation policy for Korea, followed by presentations on each project and a general discussion.
The Basic Marine Ecosystem Survey (2006–2015) examines Korea’s marine ecosystem as a whole, including seawater, sediments, and marine life. It will produce a marine-ecosystem map showing ecosystem health and provide baseline information for designating marine protected areas. The Second Coastal Wetlands Baseline Survey (2008–2012) covers coastal wetlands (tidal flats), which fall under the responsibility of the minister. Conducted every five years, it surveys the sedimentary environment, pollution, and flora and fauna of Korea’s tidal flats. In the Jeonnam region, the survey will cover the tidal flats around Shinan County, focusing on Haui-do and Sangtae-do.
The estuary survey will focus on the Yeongsan River estuary. Its scope includes estuary functions and covers water quality, the sedimentary environment, primary production, and benthic food webs. The results will serve as a basis for future economic valuation of the estuary and recommendations on policy use. The survey will also review restoration technologies and provide preliminary research for restoring small streams.
The survey area includes many islands and tidal flats, including Uido and Haui-do, with well-preserved natural scenery and high biodiversity. The ministry will consider designating areas worthy of protection or in need of conservation as protected areas, consulting local communities through public hearings.
Starting with this comprehensive marine-ecosystem survey, the ministry expects that aligning survey areas across future marine-survey projects will create synergies for environmental conservation. It aims to produce substantive, comprehensive, and interconnected findings on the local environment and establish a reliable administrative system whose results are tangible to local governments and residents.
The ministry also plans to make data from the comprehensive survey available to the public through a website. At the Ramsar Conference of the Parties in October, it plans to present project findings, including the status of tidal flats in the Jeonnam region.

ko-news-notices-401-8372c75064.title: Sihwa District Sustainable Development Council Launched as an Official Body
ko-news-notices-401-8372c75064.text:
Sihwa District Sustainable Development Council Launched as an Official Body
2022-03-02
Sihwa District Sustainable Development Council launched as an official body
A model success in collaborative governance
The Sihwa District Sustainable Development Council, which had discussed environmental improvements and eco-friendly development plans for Sihwa District, has been relaunched as an official body. The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs said it had decided that formalizing the council was necessary to strengthen its role in discussing and mediating social conflicts over improving the environment of Sihwa Lake and developing Sihwa District in an environmentally friendly way. Under the Regulation on the Prevention and Resolution of Conflicts Involving Public Institutions (a Presidential Decree), the ministry enacted the Operational Rules for the Sihwa District Sustainable Development Council (Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Directive No. 2008-43, April 8, 2008). After appointing members under those rules, it relaunched the council as an official body on April 30, 2008.
The Sihwa District Sustainable Development Council was formed in January 2004 as a public-private consultative body of civic and environmental groups, experts, relevant ministries, and local governments. It was created to resolve environmental issues in Sihwa District and conflicts over development of the Sihwa Lake tidal flats, on the principle that civic and environmental groups and the government would review all issues concerning the district’s development and environment from first principles. After holding about 160 meetings over four years, the council has achieved a number of results. Environmentally, water quality improved substantially after the project operator, the Korea Water Resources Corporation, invested about KRW 68 billion in advance for environmental improvements. Air quality also improved after residents, civic and environmental groups, and local governments jointly surveyed all approximately 2,000 businesses in the industrial complex. In urban planning, consultation and mediation enabled the Sihwa Multi-Techno Valley (MTV) and Songsan Green City projects—which had been suspended since the late 1990s amid environmental controversy—to proceed, laying a foundation for eco-friendly development.
* Improvement of river water quality in the Sihwa Industrial Complex: COD fell from 1,970 ppm in 2004 to 17 ppm in 2006.
* KRW 20 billion contributed to the Air Quality Improvement Fund for facility upgrades at major odor-emitting businesses.
* Construction of Sihwa Multi-Techno Valley (MTV), an advanced industrial complex, began on the northern tidal flats (9.26 km²) in August 2007.
* Agreement reached in August 2007 to develop Songsan Green City, a tourism and ecological complex, on the southern tidal flats (54.69 km²).
The ministry plans to ensure that the relaunched council maintains and develops its existing principle of decision-making through social consensus, communicates actively with the local community, and further broadens stakeholder participation. The chair will be jointly appointed by the private and government sides. Private-sector members will include civic and environmental groups active in Sihwa District and relevant experts recommended by those groups. Government-side members will include the Ministry for Food, Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, the Ministry of Knowledge Economy, the Ministry of Environment, and the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs; Gyeonggi Province and the cities of Siheung, Ansan, and Hwaseong; and the Korea Water Resources Corporation, the project operator for Sihwa District. To make discussions more systematic and specialized, the council will consist of a plenary meeting, a coordination committee, and expert subcommittees on urban planning and environmental improvement. When needed, it will also form a special committee to gather residents’ views and broaden community participation.
The ministry expects that the council’s official launch will make discussions more accountable and build greater trust among local residents and civil society. On that basis, it expects Sihwa District to be developed in a more environmentally friendly way.
