ko-news-notices-402-8372c75064.title: How to Lead a Team of Ten or Fewer
ko-news-notices-402-8372c75064.text:
How to Lead a Team of Ten or Fewer
2022-03-02
(How to Lead a Team of Ten or Fewer)
A team leader matters as much as a CEO!
Every company, from a small business with about ten employees to a large corporation with thousands, consists of smaller groups led by division heads, department managers, and team leaders. These group leaders set goals for employees and help them deliver results, while also doing hands-on work and delivering results themselves. In small companies, they may also act as professional managers, helping set business strategy and make decisions with the company’s executives. Their role can determine a company’s fate.
How to lead a team of ten or fewer
* Leaders do not take over their employees’ work
A person who has steadily sold cars may be promoted to team leader. If the department is told to sell 50 cars a month, how many should the leader sell? Should the leader work even harder and sell 15? The author says emphatically that a leader does not need to sell even one car personally. When leaders dive into hands-on work, they have less time to manage employees, and the employees may then fail to meet the rest of the target. A leader who exhausts themself trying to do it all may become angry, while employees lose motivation and productivity falls further. Instead, the leader should assign roles to fit employees’ personalities and abilities, then focus on motivating them and coaching them to improve their sales skills. A leader is no longer a top-performing employee; they are a department manager.
* Give clear instructions and check progress at every stage
Instructions should be expressed clearly, and progress should be checked at each stage. The key is to specify not simply “what to do,” but “what result to deliver.” Leaders should set their own expectations clearly and communicate the desired outcome to employees. As work progresses, they should check each stage and make prompt adjustments when it falls short of expectations, so the desired result can be achieved.
* Tailor support to each person’s ability and motivation
For a new employee, detailed work instructions are more urgent than personal consideration. Employees with high ability and motivation need neither close direction nor special accommodation. Unnecessary instructions or consideration can feel bothersome or signal distrust, lowering motivation.
* Do not become preoccupied with being liked
Someone who tries to win employees’ approval cannot be a good leader. The fear of being disliked clouds judgment. Staying silent when guidance is needed makes it impossible to coach employees and manage effectively. (In fact, employees are more likely to leave leaders who do not point out mistakes. By addressing mistakes clearly while also giving praise and encouragement, a leader can use both rewards and discipline flexibly.)
* Treat employees with genuine care
Genuinely caring for employees means helping them grow until they can handle any task on their own. If a leader regards employees as tools for meeting the leader’s goals or as a means of personal advancement, employees will sense it. Many people will remember how, as soon as they had that impression, their trust in the leader and their attachment to their work faded at the same time. Develop employees’ abilities as fully as possible, with the aim of helping them stand on their own after three years on the team. As they grow, the department’s productivity will be maximized—and the leader may become someone who changes an employee’s life.
Source: How to Lead a Team of Ten or Fewer (Katsuhiko Horinouchi)

ko-news-notices-403-8372c75064.title: Core Principles of Team Leadership
ko-news-notices-403-8372c75064.text:
Core Principles of Team Leadership
2022-03-02
(Team Leadership)
Only people ready to get their hands dirty can succeed as true leaders. These are the behavioral guidelines for practical, field-oriented leaders who can perform under real-world conditions.
1) Build the foundations of leadership through communication
Communication is essential to developing leadership skills; outstanding leadership cannot be exercised without it. Many businesses have failed because communication did not work smoothly. Leaders must therefore communicate effectively not only with every employee but also with business partners and customers. The heart of a communication strategy is to consistently support and encourage the organization and its members while sharing and strengthening the company’s vision.
2) Inspire people to achieve results
Leaders must be able to motivate team members to perform well. If employees are given ongoing training and opportunities to grow, and are motivated to feel recognized by their supervisors and trusted with responsibility, team performance can improve dramatically. Rather than controlling people through fear, leaders should reach them through sustained communication and motivational techniques such as positive reinforcement. Even more important, leaders must be able to motivate themselves.
3) Strengthen teamwork through coaching
Leaders also need to serve as coaches. Coaching can help employees solve problems themselves and create an environment that encourages more creative thinking. Its purpose is not simply to manage or direct employees, but to guide and influence them. Above all, leaders must not become attached to authority or formal power. Coaching produces good results through questions and discussion rather than orders, and through listening and support rather than control.
4) Delegate authority
In business, “empowerment” commonly means delegating authority. Its purpose is to help employees recognize the valuable contribution they make to the company’s growth and success. When leaders empower employees by delegating responsibilities and authority, employees can develop the ability to handle their work wisely and proactively. Unfortunately, many leaders are reluctant to accept the need to delegate. Remember that the best leaders make empowerment work by drawing fully on each employee’s potential.
5) Achieve goals through unified teamwork
As economic conditions change rapidly, companies are strengthening “team management,” forming small teams to carry out core work. They are also building stronger, more effective teamwork to achieve company goals and pursuing new directions. Team leaders should accurately understand each member’s strengths and weaknesses, recognize and make the most of their strengths, and build a dynamic team through strong teamwork.
6) Manage time effectively
Time management has become a major leadership challenge because many leaders are overwhelmed by excessive workloads. A leader who cannot organize and manage time well cannot exercise leadership effectively. Leaders should understand work priorities and schedules, use their time efficiently, and reduce their own workload as much as possible through delegation. Organizing the workspace to make work easier is another way to use time efficiently.
7) Address the causes of conflict directly
Conflict can arise in any organization, no matter how capable its leader is. Because team performance depends on how effectively conflict is resolved, leaders should quickly identify its causes and work with employees to address them. Open communication is one of the best ways to resolve conflict: ask everyone involved for their views and speak frankly with them. Most important is the courage to face the issue directly and propose a solution.
8) Take the lead in managing change
Change management is a quality closely tied to a leader’s ability to survive. In a fiercely competitive business world, believing that one can stay where one is and refuse to accept change is little more than an illusion. Leaders must understand what is changing and carefully consider how to handle the emotions and mental states that come with letting go of familiar things. How change is handled is central to change management. Open communication, trying to understand opposing viewpoints, building trust, maintaining a positive attitude, listening to employees, and delegating authority all help leaders respond to and manage change flexibly.
9) Recruit top talent
Recruiting talent is one of a leader’s key responsibilities. No strategy is better for developing an organization or company than hiring capable people; a business cannot succeed unless its human resources are combined appropriately and in balance. Hiring criteria should focus above all on candidates’ ability to contribute to the company’s success. Leaders should develop detailed hiring plans and strategies and make careful decisions. Only leaders who understand how critical recruitment is can attract top talent and ultimately build a strong workforce.
10) Develop your own approach to performance reviews
Excellent leaders regularly assess employees’ work to improve organizational productivity and results. To make reviews fair and useful, leaders should begin by accurately identifying each employee’s strengths and weaknesses and recommending ways to improve. The goal is not to criticize shortcomings but to help employees recognize them for themselves. Performance reviews should not be a one-off annual event; they should take place continuously in the ordinary course of work. It is also important to give both positive and constructive feedback and to tailor the review to each employee.
11) Leadership is tested by how well you handle problem employees
Problem employees take many forms: some lack ability, do careless work, are lazy, are always late, or openly defy company policies. Good leaders identify the type of problem and respond appropriately. When an employee causes a problem, do not rush to blame them. First show patience, acknowledge that such things can happen, and offer encouragement and support to help resolve the issue. If the problem continues, meet with the employee and ask them to correct the inappropriate behavior. If that does not work, consider dismissal carefully.
12) Recognize and reward employees’ abilities
Managing employees well is an important leadership skill: it helps them enjoy their work and sustain their desire to give their best to the leader and the company. Employee management is surprisingly often overlooked, which can cause companies irreparable losses. Leaders should actively work to retain capable employees and also take care to manage the knowledge and skills employees have built up over many years.
13) Assert yourself while respecting others
Personality is one of the most important factors in becoming a leader. Someone who does not express themselves and remains passive will never be able to lead many people.
Source: Team Leader Leadership (Bob Adams)

ko-news-notices-404-8372c75064.title: Coastal Inundation Risk Rising on the Korean Peninsula
ko-news-notices-404-8372c75064.text:
Coastal Inundation Risk Rising on the Korean Peninsula
2022-03-02
Global warming is gradually raising the risk of coastal inundation on the Korean Peninsula
An analysis found that global warming is strengthening typhoons around the Korean Peninsula and increasing annual maximum storm-surge heights.
※ Storm-surge height: the difference between the observed sea-surface height and the predicted sea level.
Since 1970, Korea’s average temperature has risen by 1.16 °C, and coastal surface-water temperatures have increased by about 0.7 °C over the past 35 years. Over the past 40 years, mean sea level in waters around Korea has also risen by approximately 2–5 mm per year, a trend that appears closely related to rising air and water temperatures.
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI), which is studying sea-level changes along the Korean coast, selected four of the country’s coastal tide-gauge sites—Yeosu, Tongyeong, Mukho, and Sokcho—and compared 20 years of observed sea-level data with meteorological data. The analysis found that maximum storm-surge heights had increased by approximately 10–30 cm. The institute determined that typhoons influenced about 78% of annual maximum storm-surge heights.
The recently released Fourth Assessment Report (2007) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) projects that during this century temperatures will rise by 1.8–4.0 °C, sea levels by 18–59 cm, and typhoons will become stronger. These projections heighten concern about extreme weather caused by rising temperatures and localized sea-level rise on the Korean Peninsula.
If a typhoon-driven storm surge coincides with high tide, severe coastal inundation could cause substantial loss of life as well as environmental and economic damage, making countermeasures urgent.
The National Oceanographic Research Institute operates oceanographic observation buoys to help forecast typhoon tracks. It plans to continue analyzing long-term changes in storm-surge height using sea-level observations, comparing those results with meteorological data, and conducting monitoring and forecasting research to reduce coastal hazards.

ko-news-notices-405-8372c75064.title: Asan Bay’s Sand Shoal Is Shifting
ko-news-notices-405-8372c75064.text:
Asan Bay’s Sand Shoal Is Shifting
2022-03-02
Comparison of 1976 and 2006 charts points to a need for research predicting seafloor changes
Localized changes in seafloor topography are actively occurring in Asan Bay.
The National Oceanographic Research Institute (NORI) compared and analyzed chart data from 1976 and 2006 and found that the form of the sand body accumulated in Asan Bay has changed over the past 30 years. The central sand shoal extends northwest to southeast from the entrance to Asan Bay for about 15 km, with a width of 2–5 km. Its northeastern side has a steeper slope than its southwestern side, giving the shoal an asymmetrical profile. The analysis found that, compared with 30 years earlier, the area of the shoal’s crest exposed above sea level at low tide had increased by about 10,000 m², and a small trough had formed at its southeastern end. The sand body had also shifted 400–500 m to the northeast, clearly showing changes in the seafloor.
Previous studies suggest that these changes resulted from changes in water-flow patterns as sea dikes, port construction, and industrial-complex development since the early 1970s made the coastline more uniform. In particular, changes in tidal-current patterns are thought to have affected the shape and direction of movement of the sand body in Asan Bay, which has a large mean tidal range (573 cm) and extends far inland. If coastal development continues, the sand body is expected to keep changing as it adjusts to the altered marine environment.
□ The National Oceanographic Research Institute plans to continue monitoring bathymetric changes to identify changes in the sand body’s shape and migration patterns and to research how seafloor topography may change in the future. It also plans to compare and analyze trends in water-depth fluctuations in areas where environmental changes are expected and produce data needed for coastal use and development, including information important to navigational safety.

ko-news-notices-406-8372c75064.title: Green Growth Through Tidal-Flat Restoration
ko-news-notices-406-8372c75064.text:
Green Growth Through Tidal-Flat Restoration
2022-03-02
Green growth through tidal-flat restoration
International symposium on tidal-flat restoration held to mark Korea’s hosting of the Ramsar Conference of the Parties
Korea’s tidal flats are counted among the world’s five largest, yet they face continuing development pressures such as landfill and reclamation.
Tidal flats are an important source of food, supplying a variety of seafood, and provide people with places to rest and enjoy beautiful scenery. They are also spawning and habitat areas for numerous marine organisms, helping sustain marine biodiversity. In addition, tidal flats are known for their strong capacities to purify pollution, prevent disasters, and regulate climate change.
As the importance of tidal flats has become more widely recognized, the need to restore damaged areas has gained attention. Large-scale restoration projects are already under way in developed countries to enhance biodiversity, recover fisheries resources, promote ecotourism, and prevent coastal disasters associated with climate change.
Taking advantage of Korea’s hosting of the 10th Ramsar Conference of the Parties, the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs is pursuing an ambitious plan to restore Korean tidal flats in an environmentally friendly way and recover marine-ecosystem functions.
The ministry announced that it would hold an international symposium on tidal-flat restoration beginning September 8 at Hoam Faculty House, Seoul National University. The theme is “Recent Progress on Coastal Wetland Restoration.” Local governments responsible for tidal flats, experts, environmental organizations, and local residents will attend.
About 200 Korean and international experts are expected. Specialists from the United States, Japan, and the Netherlands, who have extensive experience and expertise in tidal-flat restoration, will present case studies of projects in their countries. The following day, participants will visit Gochang County, which purchased a former fish farm for a restoration project, to review and advise on its tidal-flat restoration plan.
Dr. Henk J. de Vries, a Dutch expert on tidal flats in the Wadden Sea, will present a case in which reclaimed polder land in the Netherlands was restored to tidal flats. Dr. Jun Kakino of Japan will discuss reviving clam resources through restoration of tidal flats in Tokyo Bay.
The ministry plans to use the symposium to keep track of global trends in tidal-flat restoration and pursue an active restoration policy.
Yoon Hyeon-soo, Director of the ministry’s Marine Ecology Division, said, “Once the nationwide survey of damaged tidal flats and potential restoration sites is completed at the end of this year, we will establish a comprehensive restoration plan and launch a pilot project in 2009. The pilot projects under consideration include converting abandoned fish farms and salt farms back into tidal flats, as well as reversing past reclamation by restoring farmland created through reclamation.” He added, “By restoring tidal flats as a green technology, we will promote green growth through securing marine biological resources, preventing coastal disasters, and revitalizing ecotourism.”
As interest in tidal flats grows in Korea and abroad, including in connection with the Ramsar Conference of the Parties, the event is expected to draw not only specialists but also many members of the public interested in tidal flats.

ko-news-notices-407-8372c75064.title: Estuary Conservation: A Cradle of Life and a Path to a Healthy Land
ko-news-notices-407-8372c75064.text:
Estuary Conservation: A Cradle of Life and a Path to a Healthy Land
2022-03-02
Estuary conservation: a cradle of life and a path to a healthy land
Symposium to develop effective management measures for the Yeongsan River Estuary
The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs will hold a symposium on September 5 in the main conference hall of the Jeollanam-do Provincial Government Office to develop effective management measures for the Yeongsan River Estuary.
Since 2007, the ministry has been conducting systematic surveys of estuaries nationwide to establish an effective estuary-management system. This year’s survey is focused on the Yeongsan River Estuary.
In addition to the ministry’s survey results for the Yeongsan River Estuary, the symposium will discuss environmental changes, problems, and policy proposals identified by various research institutions, including the Korea Rural Community and Agriculture Corporation, the Jeonnam Development Institute, and Mokpo National University. Topics include water quality, sediments, marine life, and hydrological and hydraulic conditions. Civic groups, experts, local governments, and government agencies will use the findings as a basis for exploring ways to address the problems together.
Estuary dams have damaged ecosystems in most Korean estuaries by blocking the exchange of seawater and freshwater, destroying habitats, and disrupting food webs. In the Yeongsan River Estuary, environmental problems—including continued deterioration in water quality and damage to the estuary ecosystem—have occurred since the estuary dam was built in 1981.
The water in the inner Yeongsan Lake, cut off by the estuary dam, is now unsuitable even for irrigation. Eutrophication is also worsening its effects on the ecosystem, including algal blooms in Mokpo Port near the dam. Effective management measures to improve water quality are urgently needed.
Yoon Hyeon-su, Director of the Marine Ecology Division at the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs, said, “Existing estuary policies were considered to have achieved substantial results in securing a stable water supply, producing food, and building transport infrastructure. However, as social issues and values have changed, various problems, including ecosystem destruction, have come to light. This symposium will present expert assessments of the Yeongsan River Estuary’s current conditions and problems, then provide an open forum for local residents, local governments, NGOs, and other stakeholders to develop solutions together. We will discuss a range of measures, including restoring estuaries and improving water quality through renewed seawater exchange.”
Based on the proposals made at the symposium, the ministry plans to develop and implement more effective estuary-management policies through cooperation between central and local governments.

ko-news-notices-408-8372c75064.title: The Seven Habits of Successful People
ko-news-notices-408-8372c75064.text:
The Seven Habits of Successful People
2022-03-02
(Overview of the Seven Habits of Successful People)
1) Habit 1: Be proactive
Our actions are the result of the choices we make; they are not determined by the circumstances around us.
- “There’s nothing I can do” → “Let’s look for alternatives.”
- “He makes me so angry” → “I can manage my emotions.”
- “They won’t let me” → “I can persuade them effectively.”
2) Habit 2: Set goals and take action (personal leadership)
Starting today, use the image, character, and perspective you want to have at the end of your life as the frame of reference and standard for examining everything you do.
3) Habit 3: Put what matters first (the principle of personal management)
Successful people are willing to do the things others do not want to do.
“The most important things must never be at the mercy of the least important.” (Goethe)
- The ability to prepare and plan according to priorities
- The ability to act according to priorities
4) Habit 4: Seek mutual benefit (interpersonal leadership)
Adopt a mindset that seeks mutual benefit in every interpersonal relationship.
5) Habit 5: Seek first to understand, then to be understood (the principle of empathetic communication)
6) Habit 6: Use synergy (the principle of productive cooperation)
This is the most difficult habit to put into practice.
Many people have never experienced even a little synergy at home or at work. They have been trained to communicate defensively and protectively, and conditioned by the idea that they should not trust other people or life itself. As a result, they are not open to productive cooperation. This is one of life’s greatest tragedies and wastes: enormous potential is buried and never developed.
* Example of synergy: generating a new idea in a classroom or organization
- First, an atmosphere emerges in which people open up to one another, learn from one another’s ideas, listen, and feel safe. → Brainstorming follows, with creativity, imagination, and intellectual exchange taking precedence over judgment and criticism. → A discussion then weaves the ideas together and builds on them, leading to new progress, ideas, and exciting change that everyone involved can clearly see.
7) Habit 7: Renew your mind and body (balanced self-renewal)

ko-news-notices-409-8372c75064.text:
Gyeongin Canal Project Plan
2022-03-02
The plan proposes using a flood diversion channel as a canal to prevent floods, reduce logistics costs and traffic congestion, promote culture, tourism, and leisure, and support regional economic development.
□ The Gyeongin Canal would also serve as a flood diversion channel, helping prevent flood damage in the Gulpocheon basin, which is prone to repeated inundation, during a flood with a 100-year return period.

ko-news-notices-410-8372c75064.title: Red and Green Tides Reach the Waters off Jeju Island
ko-news-notices-410-8372c75064.text:
Red and Green Tides Reach the Waters off Jeju Island
2022-03-02
Red and Green Tides Reach the Waters off Jeju Island
Part 2: Effects of the Three Gorges Dam (Dong-rim Choi, Principal Researcher, South Sea Characteristics Research Division)
The Yangtze River basin is a catchment area into which water from all tributaries flows to the main channel. It covers about 1,940,000 km², one-fifth of China’s land area, and is home to about 400 million people—roughly one-third of China’s population. Compared with South Korea’s area (100,000 km²) and population (48 million), the basin is about 19 times larger and has more than eight times as many residents, respectively. Material washed by rain from its mountains and plains—including loess—as well as substances dissolved in surface water and groundwater all flow into the Yangtze’s main channel. The river is far more turbid than what people generally picture as river water: its murky yellow-brown, loess-like color makes its high suspended-sediment content readily apparent. Domestic sewage, agricultural and livestock wastewater, and industrial wastewater from the basin’s cities and towns also flow into the Yangtze.
About 50,000 large and small dams have been built on the Yangtze’s main channel and tributaries. The Three Gorges Dam, by far the world’s largest in terms of size, freshwater storage, and power-generation capacity, was scheduled for completion in 2009. It is about 2.3 km wide and 185 m high. Its reservoir extends to Chongqing, with an average width of about 1.1 km and a length of about 660 km; its maximum storage capacity is about 39.3 billion tonnes. A major problem with impounding Yangtze water is that its high concentration of suspended sediment settles on the reservoir bed. Before the dam was built, this suspended sediment formed natural levees as it moved downstream and helped create new land when it reached the coast near the Yangtze Estuary and Shanghai.
Sites where a low-salinity water mass from the Yangtze and patches of red tide to the west and green tide algae (Ulva prolifera) to the east were observed during marine observations in waters southwest of Jeju Island, August 1–5, 2008. The inset at the upper right shows the Yangtze River basin.
The Yangtze discharges an average of about 480 million tonnes of sediment into the East China Sea each year. However, as dam construction accelerated in the 1980s, suspended-sediment concentrations began to decline noticeably. Chinese data show that, during the three years from completion of the Three Gorges Dam’s first-stage impoundment works in 2003 to completion of the second-stage works in 2006, the reservoir level rose from 136 m to 156 m. During that period, the average annual sediment discharge fell sharply to about 170 million tonnes. In 2006 alone, it dropped to a striking 90 million tonnes—less than 100 million.
When construction was scheduled to be completed in 2009 and the reservoir level to rise to 175 m, sediment discharge was expected to decline even further. Plans for more dams were expected to accelerate the reduction. Discharge was also expected to decline further once the South-to-North Water Diversion Project, then under construction, was completed. The project was a large-scale system of artificial waterways intended to carry water from the Yangtze in the south to water-scarce areas in the north. For comparison, the Yellow River had typically discharged about 1 billion tonnes of suspended sediment, but that amount fell sharply in the 2000s; it was reported that only about 12% of the historical volume was still reaching the Bohai Sea.
In addition to suspended sediment, the Yangtze carries nutrients to the estuary and coastal waters and into the East China Sea. Major nutrients—including nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and silicon (Si)—dissolve in freshwater and are delivered to the sea. Chinese reports show that nitrate and phosphate concentrations in the Yangtze Estuary have risen sharply since the mid-1980s. The reported causes include excessive use of chemical fertilizers to increase agricultural production, rising domestic wastewater discharges such as those containing synthetic detergents, and indiscriminate release of industrial wastewater—problems common to modern industrial societies. By contrast, silicate concentrations have clearly declined. Dam construction reduces the supply of land-derived silicate to the sea, and the sharp drop in suspended-sediment discharge caused by the Three Gorges Dam is expected to further accelerate the decline of silicate in the East China Sea.
The quantity and balance of nutrients in marine ecosystems strongly affect the community structure and species composition of phytoplankton. Excess nitrogen and phosphorus from land can cause eutrophication in coastal waters, leading to large blooms of harmful red-tide organisms. Red-tide events and affected areas in the Yangtze Estuary and nearby coastal waters have reportedly increased rapidly since the 1990s, owing to abundant nitrate and phosphate. In contrast, silicate supply is declining, and studies report a gradual decrease in the share of diatoms—which depend on silicate—in the overall phytoplankton community. These ecosystem changes are viewed as an environmental anomaly: a balance formed as organisms adapted over millions of years is being disrupted in an extremely short time by human activities driven by self-interest.
This year’s observed green tide and red tide are distributed to the east and west, respectively, of the Yangtze’s low-salinity water mass. In other words, the green tide leads and the red tide follows. The low-salinity water mass flowing out of the Yangtze Estuary served as a carrier, transporting algae that had been present in the estuary and coastal areas. Last year, DDT—a persistent organic pollutant—was detected at concentrations far higher than those in surrounding seawater in a relatively low-salinity water mass, about 30‰, observed west of Jeju. China used the third-largest amount of DDT in the world, after the United States and the former Soviet Union. Although DDT use is now banned in both Korea and China, legacy DDT that does not readily degrade appears to remain mixed into Yangtze water and to travel with it. This indicates that harmful organisms and hazardous chemical pollutants are not confined to the Yangtze Estuary and its coastal waters; they are also carried by low-salinity water into Korean waters.
The Yangtze supplies an average of about 920 billion tonnes of freshwater to the East China Sea each year. More than half—about 480 billion tonnes—flows out during the rainy season from June through September, about 25 times the discharge of the Nakdong River. A substantial amount can reach Jeju Island, about 450 km from the Yangtze Estuary, in roughly one month. Large water-management projects centered on the Yangtze, including the Three Gorges Dam, are also bringing rapid changes in water quality and the environment. These environmental changes are too close to Korean waters, too large in scale, and too clearly consequential to treat as problems confined within a neighboring country. What is needed now is a systematic approach to the rapidly changing regional environment: examine it closely, diagnose it accurately, and develop appropriate responses.
I will close by hoping that the red and green tides that appeared in Jeju waters this year are a temporary phenomenon, rather than a sign of environmental changes that could make such events recur regularly.
Source: Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute (KORDI), September 22, 2008

ko-news-notices-411-8372c75064.title: Inaugural General Meeting of the Korea Maritime Enterprises Association
ko-news-notices-411-8372c75064.text:
Inaugural General Meeting of the Korea Maritime Enterprises Association
2022-03-02
- Creating a blue ocean by strengthening cooperation among small and medium-sized maritime enterprises -
To strengthen business competitiveness by promoting exchange and cooperation among small and medium-sized maritime enterprises, the inaugural general meeting of the Korea Maritime Enterprises Association, joined by 79 maritime-related companies, will be held at the Ritz-Carlton Hotel in Seoul at 3 p.m. on Wednesday, December 17.
About 100 people, including Lee Jae-gyun, Vice Minister of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs, National Assembly member Park Sang-eun, and representatives of member companies, will attend the meeting. The association will hold its promoters' meeting and begin official activities.
The newly launched Korea Maritime Enterprises Association is a private-sector-led consultative body. It plans to support the continued growth of the maritime industry by sharing maritime-related information and proposing policies to strengthen business competitiveness.
An official from the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs said, ‘The launch of the Korea Maritime Enterprises Association is expected to help small maritime businesses overcome the limitations they have faced and promote the development of the maritime industry through cooperation among companies. It is also significant that, amid recent difficult economic conditions, maritime business owners have voluntarily formed an association in a spirit of mutual support, resolved to overcome the crisis wisely and make a fresh start.’
Source: Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Policy News, 2008-12-17, 6:00 a.m.

ko-news-notices-412-8372c75064.title: Gageocho Marine Science Base Scheduled for Completion in Early October
ko-news-notices-412-8372c75064.text:
Gageocho Marine Science Base Scheduled for Completion in Early October
2022-03-02
- Korea's second marine science base, following the Ieodo base -
The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs (Minister Jeong Jong-hwan) announced that it would invest KRW 5.9 billion the following year (out of a total construction cost of KRW 10 billion) to complete the Gageocho Marine Science Base in October. This will make Gageocho the country's second comprehensive marine science base, following the Ieodo Marine Science Base, completed in 2003.
The science base is being installed on Gageocho, 47 km west of Gageodo, in water 15 m deep. The base structure is currently being fabricated on land. As of December 2008, construction was about 40% complete.
The Gageocho base will stand about 51 m tall, with 26 m—roughly the height of a 10-story apartment building—rising above the water. It will weigh 523 tonnes and cover 330 m² (100 pyeong), about one-quarter the size of the Ieodo base. Although smaller than the Ieodo base, it will not differ greatly in function.
The Gageocho base will be equipped with 27 types of meteorological and oceanographic instruments. Observation data will be transmitted in real time via the Mugunghwa satellite to relevant researchers.
The transmitted observations are expected to improve the accuracy of weather and marine forecasts and to be used in many areas, including minimizing damage from natural disasters at sea.
Source: Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs, 2008-12-29, 11:00 a.m.

ko-news-notices-413-8372c75064.title: Deep-Sea Hydrothermal Vent Microbes to Power the World
ko-news-notices-413-8372c75064.text:
Deep-Sea Hydrothermal Vent Microbes to Power the World
2022-03-02
- Ministry opens a path to highly efficient hydrogen production using hyperthermophilic archaea -
<Deep-sea hydrothermal vent>
The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs (Minister Jeong Jong-hwan) announced that it had, for the first time in Korea, developed core technology for producing highly efficient biohydrogen using the hyperthermophilic archaeon NA1 (Thermococcus onnurineus NA1), isolated from a deep-sea hydrothermal vent in the South Pacific.
The research is considered a major achievement of the Marine Biotechnology Development Program, which the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs has been pursuing as its own R&D program.
* Research institution: Marine and Extreme Biomolecular Genome Research Center (Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute; President: Kang Jeong-geuk)
NA1 is an archaeon that grows at 80°C. It was collected in 2002 from a hydrothermal vent field off Papua New Guinea by Korea's oceanographic research vessel Onnuri.
Genome analysis found that NA1 has eight hydrogenase gene clusters—at least twice as many as those reported in other microorganisms to date. This is associated with a much higher hydrogen yield per unit, and the organism can produce biohydrogen using a wide range of substrates, including carbon monoxide (CO), starch, and formate.
NA1 can also be cultured using environmental pollutants such as carbon monoxide as a substrate. This is expected to offer a significant way to reduce carbon monoxide emissions from companies whose manufacturing processes release it.
A team led by Dr. Sangjin Kim at the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute published the findings in the November 2008 issue of the internationally respected Journal of Bacteriology (impact factor 4.0; among the top 10% in microbiology). A domestic patent application had been filed, and international applications were being prepared.
According to a recent economic analysis*, producing 1 kg of hydrogen from carbon monoxide using NA1 was estimated to cost $0.80, making it more economical than other methods, such as water splitting, that cost more than $3 per kilogram.
The article forecast that commercialization could be possible within five years if further research** continued on gene-regulation mechanisms and production-optimization conditions.
* Jointly conducted by Ensoltech Co., Ltd., the Korea Institute of Energy Research, the Korea Basic Science Institute, Kyung Hee University, and Sogang University.
** Research to maximize hydrogen production efficiency by identifying the conditions under which hydrogenase gene clusters are expressed or suppressed, or through genetic manipulation.
Hydrogen can produce heat and electricity through a simple electrochemical reaction with oxygen in the air. Because its only by-product is water (H2O), it is regarded as an environmentally friendly future energy source that does not emit CO2.
Hydrogen also has a high calorific value per unit weight and can be used in almost every field of today's energy systems, including as a basic industrial material and as a general fuel, and in automobiles, aircraft, and fuel cells. However, current hydrogen-production technologies rely on fossil fuels in the water-splitting process and yield little hydrogen relative to the energy input, making them economically unviable. This creates a need to develop hydrogen-production technologies using solar power, wind power, and microorganisms.
The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs said it planned to begin pilot production in 2009 by further elucidating the hydrogen-production mechanism and establishing a high-efficiency strain-production system.
Source: Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs Policy News, 2008-12-11, 11:00 a.m.

ko-news-notices-414-8372c75064.title: Cheong Wa Dae Creates Regional Development Secretary Post for Four Rivers Restoration
ko-news-notices-414-8372c75064.text:
Cheong Wa Dae Creates Regional Development Secretary Post for Four Rivers Restoration
2022-03-02
Cheong Wa Dae Creates Regional Development Secretary Post for Four Rivers Restoration
On the 21st, Cheong Wa Dae carried out an organizational reshuffle and follow-up appointments at the secretary level, including the creation of a regional development secretary post responsible for comprehensive regional development measures and the Four Rivers Restoration Project.
Oh Jeong-gyu, head of the planning team at the National Balanced Development Committee, was appointed to the newly created regional development secretary post under the Senior Secretary to the President for State Affairs Planning. After being appointed in May as the second secretary for national policy projects under that senior secretary's office, Oh was reassigned following the Cheong Wa Dae reorganization. The Senior Secretary to the President for State Affairs Planning will therefore have four secretaries responsible for government policy, future vision, broadcasting and communications, and regional development.
The post of secretary for national policy projects under the Senior Secretary to the President for State Affairs Planning had become vacant when its incumbent, Heo Gyeong-wook, was appointed vice minister of the Ministry of Strategy and Finance. The post was renamed secretary for government affairs, and Kim Dong-yeon, previously secretary for economic and financial affairs, was appointed to it.
The secretary for economic and financial affairs post was also renamed secretary for economic affairs, and Lim Jong-ryong, director of the Planning and Coordination Office at the Ministry of Strategy and Finance, was appointed. Cheong Wa Dae was also reported to be setting up a separate finance team in the form of a task force under the Senior Secretary to the President for Economic Affairs, with a secretary-level team leader to be appointed later. The finance secretary post, eliminated in the organizational reshuffle the previous June, was effectively being restored after seven months. The reported view was that the new finance team reflected the judgment that financial-market stability was essential to addressing the economic downturn and corporate restructuring, which were top government priorities that year.
Cheong Wa Dae also renamed the secretary for science as secretary for science and technology, the first deputy spokesperson as deputy spokesperson, and the second deputy spokesperson as director of the Chunchugwan press center.
A Cheong Wa Dae official explained, “We carried out a partial reorganization to respond actively to changing circumstances, including the economic crisis, and to support the smooth conduct of state affairs, including the pursuit of a new government agenda. We have improved efficiency by creating posts or strengthening functions only where necessary.”
Reporter Choi Jae-wang, jwchoi@msnet.co.kr

ko-news-notices-415-8372c75064.title: Four Rivers Restoration: A New Starting Point for Creating Ecological Rivers
ko-news-notices-415-8372c75064.text:
Four Rivers Restoration: A New Starting Point for Creating Ecological Rivers
2022-03-02
Four Rivers Restoration: A New Starting Point for Creating Ecological Rivers
The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs is preparing guidelines for creating ecological rivers.
The Four Rivers Restoration Project is expected to mark a new direction for river development in Korea: preserving the natural functions of rivers and transforming them into genuine ecological rivers where life thrives.
As it carries out the Four Rivers Restoration Project, the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs is preparing Guidelines for Ecological River Development Plans to preserve the natural functions of rivers, create ecological rivers suited to their natural characteristics, and conserve the river environment.
The new guidelines will require plans to reflect the ecological characteristics of each river and to gather and incorporate the views of local residents and experts from the planning stage, particularly when developing river areas for public use. Based on thorough surveys, including analysis and assessment of the river's characteristics, the guidelines will set different planning directions for conservation, restoration, and water-friendly zones so that the continuity and diversity of the river as a whole can be preserved.
Conservation zones are areas with outstanding ecological, historical, cultural, or scenic value that should be preserved without artificial modification. As a rule, artificial environmental changes or structural alterations will be prohibited there in order to conserve each river's natural characteristics.
Restoration zones are areas damaged or destroyed by human interference or natural disasters that require restoration to conserve their natural, historical, or cultural value. Their past and present conditions will be reviewed together, and flood control, water use, and landscape will be assessed comprehensively. Restoration will be carried out only to the extent that it does not undermine the conservation of the river's natural characteristics.
Water-friendly zones are near densely populated areas or city centers, where water-related recreational activities can take place for public benefit as long as the river's inherent value is not compromised. These zones will be managed to conserve and restore the river's environmental functions and foster a desirable relationship between the river and people's lives.
Facilities installed in water-friendly zones must minimize ecological disturbance, avoid concrete structures, and use natural or environmentally friendly materials for paved surfaces.
To avoid affecting flood conveyance and water flow, the installation of fixed facilities will be restricted, with benches, lighting, and small sports facilities as exceptions. The guidelines will also address restrictions on excessive sports facilities through facility-layout plans in water-friendly zones, prohibit parking lots along rivers, and include bicycle paths.
The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs is revising the draft Guidelines for Ecological River Development Plans after gathering opinions and advice from experts in various fields. It plans to finalize the guidelines by the end of this month and send them to local governments and regional land management offices for application to the Four Rivers Restoration Project. If the approach proves effective, the Ministry plans to expand the guidelines to other river-development projects, giving greater priority to ecological-river conservation than to water-friendly areas.

ko-news-notices-416-8372c75064.title: Gangwon Deep Water's ‘Cheonnyeon Dongan’ to Launch in May
ko-news-notices-416-8372c75064.text:
Gangwon Deep Water's ‘Cheonnyeon Dongan’ to Launch in May
2022-03-02
Gangwon Deep Water Co., Ltd. (CEO Go Myeong-seon) has completed its deep ocean water production plant and held a completion ceremony on April 17 at its headquarters in Goseong County. About 200 guests from Korea and abroad attended, including Gangwon Province Governor Kim Jin-seon, Goseong County Governor Hwang Jong-guk, Daekyo Group Chairman Kang Young-jung, and Matsuo Masaki, chairman of Japan's KIBI System.
In November of the previous year, Gangwon Deep Water installed an offshore platform capable of taking in 3,000 tonnes of deep ocean water per day, 6 km offshore in the East Sea at a depth of 605 m. It also installed what it described as Korea's only seamless deep-ocean-water intake pipe, enabling a stable supply of raw water. With the completion of an onshore plant that includes a facility capable of desalinating 90 tonnes per day and bottle-manufacturing and packaging equipment, the company now has an advanced production facility that can handle the entire process, from water intake to finished products, at one site.
The completed plant provides a system for using deep ocean water from raw intake water through desalinated water to mineral water. The company plans to ramp up product manufacturing in May and begin selling its drinkable deep ocean water, ‘Cheonnyeon Dongan’ (literally, ‘For a Thousand Years’), in June.
The newly launched product will come in two sizes: 1.2 L for home delivery and 350 mL for retail outlets. For home delivery, the company will recruit members among households that purchase water purifiers and bottled water, then deliver directly to their homes. The price is KRW 1,000 per bottle. The retail product will be available through department stores, hotels, fitness clubs, convenience stores, and other outlets at KRW 800 per bottle.
What is deep ocean water?
It is a seawater resource that originates in Greenland and circulates through the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans on a 2,000-year cycle. When the circulating seawater reaches Greenland's glacial region, it becomes very cold and denser, then sinks into the deep sea (water at depths below 200 m). The water, cooled to about 2°C, remains separated from water near the surface, forming a boundary and not mixing with it, like oil and water. This is called ‘deep ocean water.’
The deep ocean water on the seafloor of the East Sea off Goseong County, Gangwon Province, is said to have formed near Greenland about 4,000 years ago. The article describes it as clean, with excellent self-purification capacity and abundant minerals, and as a promising new resource for use in diverse industries.
In particular, the deep ocean water off Goseong, drawn from a depth of 605 m, was found to contain abundant minerals considered beneficial to the human body, including magnesium, calcium, potassium, and sodium.

ko-news-notices-417-8372c75064.title: Incheon to Co-Develop Tidal-Current Power Facilities with Private Companies
ko-news-notices-417-8372c75064.text:
Incheon to Co-Develop Tidal-Current Power Facilities with Private Companies
2022-03-02
Incheon City said on the 20th that it was considering jointly developing tidal-current power facilities with a private company, using seawater flows in waters near Deokjeokdo.
The Deokjeokdo tidal-current power project is planned as a public-private third-sector development. POSCO Engineering & Construction will manufacture the equipment and develop the site; Korea South-East Power Co., Ltd. will build and operate the system; and Inha University will provide technical advice.
The city plans to sign a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with these organizations on the 29th and then finalize a detailed project schedule, with operation targeted for 2016.
A proposal now under consideration calls for investing KRW 800 billion to install 200 tidal-current turbines at four sites around Deokjeokdo, Daeijakdo, and Soijakdo off the Incheon coast. Each turbine would have a capacity of 1 MW, and together they could generate 613,200 MW of electricity per year. That would equal 3.2% of Incheon's current annual electricity demand of 18,165,000 MW.
The city expects the project to displace, each year, power-generation fuel equivalent to 212,642 tonnes of bituminous coal, 126,511 tonnes of heavy oil, and 101,414 tonnes of liquefied natural gas (LNG).

ko-news-notices-418-8372c75064.title: Jeju Naval Base Construction Faces Serious Obstacles; Conflict Continues
ko-news-notices-418-8372c75064.text:
Jeju Naval Base Construction Faces Serious Obstacles; Conflict Continues
2022-03-02
(Jeju = Yonhap News) Reporter Kim Seung-beom — Next month will mark two years since Jeju Province decided to accept the government's plan to build a naval base on Jeju, which had sparked sharp controversy among residents. Yet the conflict over the project shows no signs of abating.
On the 20th, residents of Gangjeong Village in Seogwipo and civil-society groups opposing the naval base filed a suit with the Seoul Administrative Court seeking to revoke the approval, arguing that the Minister of National Defense's approval in January of the implementation plan for the naval-base project violated the Environmental Impact Assessment Act. On the 21st, they held a rally in front of the Jeju Provincial Government building and declared their determination to fight to the end.
The Navy Headquarters, the project operator, is pressing ahead with its original schedule, which targets a December groundbreaking. It is proceeding with the land-compensation plan and publishing the draft environmental impact assessment.
Supporters argue that the naval-base project is a national undertaking that will help revitalize the local economy; opponents say it will tarnish Jeju's image as an Island of Peace and harm its clean ecosystem. The project had been discussed several times from 2001 onward and became official in April 2007, when the Minister of National Defense visited Jeju and conveyed the government's position.
The administration of Jeju Governor Kim Tae-hwan had been weighing how to resolve the naval-base issue, which became prominent during the 2006 local elections. As soon as Kim's term began in July that year, his administration decided that it would make a policy decision after comprehensively assessing three prerequisites for construction: ‘consensus among Jeju residents,’ ‘compatibility with the Island of Peace image,’ and ‘contribution to the local economy.’
In May of the following year, Governor Kim endorsed the government's plan to build the naval base, saying, ‘An analysis by the civilian-government task force on the naval base found that the naval base and the Island of Peace can coexist and that construction would have a substantial ripple effect on the local economy.’
He also announced the results of public-opinion surveys. In a survey of 1,500 Jeju residents commissioned by the Jeju Association for Local Autonomy Studies and conducted by Gallup Korea on whether to host a naval base, 54.3% supported it and 38.2% opposed it—a 16.1-percentage-point lead for supporters. In a separate survey of 1,000 residents in each of the three towns and townships being considered as candidate sites, Daecheon-dong, which includes Gangjeong Village, had 56% support, compared with 42.2% in Andeok-myeon, and was selected as the top-priority site.
Some Gangjeong residents, civil-society groups, religious groups, and others opposing the base then questioned whether a telephone poll was the only way for provincial authorities to ascertain residents' views when deciding the policy for a naval base that had been controversial for as long as 15 years. They raised successive objections about whether a sample of 1,500 was representative of residents and whether the polling process was objective.
The Jeju Provincial Council's Special Committee on Military Bases also conducted an administrative investigation into the poll. It pointed to inadequate survey questions, ambiguity in the weighting methodology, and compromised neutrality resulting from Navy briefings held in each village in Daecheon-dong, Seogwipo.
Around this time, Hyun Ae-ja, a Democratic Labor Party lawmaker from Jeju, staged a 27-day hunger strike to protest what she called the unfairness of the policy decision. The Jeju Diocese of the Catholic Church's priests formed a ‘Special Committee for the Island of Peace’ and publicized their opposition to hosting a military base. Opposition campaigns continued across different sectors of society.
As opposition to the naval-base construction grew stronger, the government and political circles shifted toward considering a combined port that would add ‘tourist port’ and ‘cruise port’ functions to the naval base.
The Korea Development Institute (KDI), which conducted a commissioned study, said that adding berthing facilities for ultra-large cruise ships to the planned naval-base breakwater, building a new access road, and adding a tourist park featuring naval vessels, a cruise terminal, and an outdoor park near Gangjeong Port would yield a benefit-to-cost ratio of 1.4, above the 1.0 threshold. KDI judged the proposal economically feasible.
On that basis, the Prime Minister's Office announced, following a National Policy Coordination Meeting in September of the previous year, a plan to develop a ‘world-class civilian-military complex tourist port on the coast of Gangjeong Village, Seogwipo, Jeju Island.’ It changed the planned naval base's designation to a ‘civilian-military complex.’
Under the development plan now finalized, the Navy will invest KRW 953.7 billion by 2014 to build a 1,950 m pier in the Gangjeong Village area, covering 480,000 m² (including 200,000 m² of reclaimed public waters). The pier will be able to berth about 20 naval vessels and two 150,000-ton cruise ships simultaneously. The plan also includes support facilities for about 7,500 military personnel and their families.
The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs plans to spend KRW 53.4 billion on cruise-ship berthing facilities, a terminal, and a naval-vessel-themed park at the site. It also plans to coordinate with Jeju Province on additional support under a regional comprehensive development plan scheduled for completion in May.
The Ministry of National Defense subsequently pursued prior environmental review consultations with the Ministry of Environment for the civilian-military complex tourist port, secured KRW 37.5 billion in the 2009 budget, and proceeded with bidding for the port construction. In January, it approved the implementation plan for the national defense and military facilities project (Jeju Naval Base), naming the Chief of Naval Operations as the project operator.
The government argues that the Jeju Naval Base is necessary, saying, ‘To defend the country and protect the southern sea routes, and for Jeju to prosper as an international hub for exchange and cooperation and as an international free city, it is essential to secure the means of self-defense needed to protect peace from external threats.’
Opponents counter, ‘If a naval base is built, it could become a focal point or target in a military conflict in an emergency, and there is a risk of damaging Jeju's image as an Island of Peace and an international resort destination.’
They strongly oppose the project, saying that reclaiming public waters for the base is expected to damage the marine environment and fishing rights, including those associated with village fishing grounds, while bringing little benefit to the local economy.
They also raised concerns about the quality of the joint ecological survey of the Gangjeong waters in February. They said the survey period was limited and the survey area covered only the area extending 3.5 km offshore from the Gangjeong-dong shoreline, as proposed by the Navy, making it difficult to properly assess the ecological status of the soft-coral communities.
The Navy Headquarters has continued to push the project forward: last month it announced a compensation plan for 201 parcels of land to be expropriated, totaling about 284,000 m²; on the 6th of this month it published the draft environmental impact assessment; and it scheduled a briefing for residents on the 24th. Without special measures, a confrontation between the two sides appears inevitable.

ko-news-notices-419-8372c75064.title: ‘Dams May Actually Worsen Water Quality’: Four Rivers Project Meets a Countercurrent
ko-news-notices-419-8372c75064.text:
‘Dams May Actually Worsen Water Quality’: Four Rivers Project Meets a Countercurrent
2022-03-02
The Four Rivers Maintenance Project has encountered an unexpected obstacle: water quality. The government's official position is that dredging the four rivers and building weirs (low dams) will increase the volume of water and thereby improve water quality. But an analysis within the government has raised the possibility that this may not be the case.
On the 21st, sources at the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs and the Ministry of Environment said the government was reportedly pursuing a plan to secure more water in the four rivers by building about ten weirs, each no more than 15 m high: two or three on the Han River, five or six on the Nakdong River, and the remainder across the other rivers.
The question is how weirs will affect water quality. Until now, the Ministry of Land had argued that water quality would ‘improve,’ while environmental groups and others argued it would ‘worsen.’ The Ministry of Environment, the lead agency for water-quality management, had not stated its position.
At an internal Ministry of Environment meeting on the 15th, chaired by Minister Lee Man-eui and titled the ‘Meeting on Measures to Restore River Health in the Four Major Rivers,’ the ministry's National Institute of Environmental Research (NIER) presented an analysis concluding that water quality would worsen if about ten weirs were built across the four rivers.
NIER conducted the simulation after receiving some data, including a water-quality forecasting model, from the Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology. The institute was carrying out, at the Ministry of Land's request, a commissioned study to prepare the master plan (basic plan) for the Four Rivers Maintenance Project.
According to government sources, the analysis found that installing weirs could have a beneficial effect by increasing water volume and diluting pollutants, thereby reducing pollution levels. However, the negative effect of impeding water flow and raising pollution levels was greater.
More specifically, total phosphorus (TP) concentrations fell to some extent as phosphorus was trapped behind weirs and settled on the riverbed. However, chlorophyll-a, associated with algal growth and green-water blooms, and biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) showed ‘an overall tendency to increase,’ according to multiple government sources.
For example, annual BOD in Paldang Lake on the Han River was 1.2 ppm in 2007 and 1.3 ppm in 2008. The sources said water quality would remain unchanged or become worse even after the river-improvement project, including weir construction, was completed.
A government official said, ‘This means that even if we spend KRW 14 trillion to complete work on the four rivers by 2012, then invest several trillion won more in water-quality improvement measures, water quality still will not improve.’
That would undermine the government's long-term water-quality management plan at its foundation. Some within the government have consequently voiced concern that ‘the Four Rivers Project could follow the path of Sihwa Lake and Saemangeum.’
At Sihwa Lake, water pollution rose rapidly to an unexpected level as the reservoir was being filled with freshwater after the seawall was completed. After the water became severely polluted, the outcome was to open the seawall gates and allow seawater to circulate through the lake. Saemangeum also became the subject of intense debate after a Ministry of Environment analysis found that its freshwater reservoir would be difficult to use as agricultural water meeting Grade 4 standards. The concern is that the Four Rivers Maintenance Project could also hit a water-quality obstacle.
These findings are still preliminary and may change. Yoon Seung-jun, director general of the Ministry of Environment's Water Environment Policy Bureau, said, ‘This is a forecast made before the master plan has been finalized, so we cannot conclude that building weirs will worsen water quality.’
Je Hae-chi, head of the public-relations team at the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs' Four Rivers Planning Headquarters, also said, ‘Nothing has been finalized about how many weirs will be built on the four rivers or how high they will be.’ Some observers noted that water-quality issues related to the weirs could be raised at the ‘Four Rivers Restoration Report Session’ chaired by President Lee Myung-bak on the 27th, and that the outcome could prove a turning point for the Four Rivers Project.

ko-news-notices-427-8372c75064.title: Keep Working Cheerfully to the End
ko-news-notices-427-8372c75064.text:
Keep Working Cheerfully to the End
2022-03-02
We all face personal difficulties. Some of us are physically ill; many of us also have a host of mentally exhausting concerns. When social and economic conditions are poor, stress rises further. If we do not face that stress calmly, we may react more strongly than necessary and waste our precious mental energy. In his book *The Illusory Brain*, Yuji Ikegaya wrote, ‘It is important to know how to relieve stress, but we also need the mindset to face stress with confidence and the belief that we can relieve it whenever it arises.’
Even when we face personal difficulties and stress, we still have things to do and goals to pursue. That can be truly difficult. Yet these are precisely the times when we need the perseverance to keep going until we have established a firm footing. Anselm Grün wrote in his book *Don't Stay; Keep Flowing*:

‘Keep at whatever you do until you have put down roots where you chose to be. I very much want to see you grow.’

When you face a difficult challenge, it may be hard and exhausting, but it is important to do your best until you have established a solid foundation for the work. Once that foundation is in place, things will go more smoothly. The results of the work can then be substantial. As you keep working through hardship until you have established that foundation, it is important to have confidence that you can face and relieve the stress along the way. We are told that we have only one life, so we need to do our best in each moment. It is an obvious yet precious truth that we live by helping one another, together with our family and friends. Even in difficult times, we should live joyfully, bringing joy to ourselves and to those who love us, and receiving joy in return.
Source: Hyundai Research Institute, 2009-07-24

ko-news-notices-428-8372c75064.title: Marine Observations Conducted at the Entrance to the Gyeongin Ara Waterway
ko-news-notices-428-8372c75064.text:
Marine Observations Conducted at the Entrance to the Gyeongin Ara Waterway
2022-03-02
The National Oceanographic Research Institute conducted marine observations at the entrance to the Gyeongin Ara Waterway from April 1 to May 15 and announced the results.
To determine seawater movement, the Institute mounted advanced marine-observation equipment (RCM-9) on a buoy and collected data for 30 days, from April 14 to May 13. The analysis found that currents flowed along a north–south axis and reached a maximum speed of 2.6 knots.
An Institute official said, ‘The data collected can serve as baseline information for analyzing changes in the surrounding environment before and after construction of the Gyeongin Ara Waterway and the passage of vessels. We plan to conduct periodic observations to provide accurate data in the future.’
The National Oceanographic Research Institute said it would publish the project results on its website (www.nori.go.kr).

ko-news-notices-429-8372c75064.title: Master Plan for National Rivers Outside the Four Major Rivers
ko-news-notices-429-8372c75064.text:
Master Plan for National Rivers Outside the Four Major Rivers
2022-03-02
The Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs (Minister Jeong Jong-hwan) announced that it would launch a commissioned study on July 23 to prepare a master plan for national rivers other than the four major rivers. The plan aims to reshape these rivers as places that are safer from floods and rich in water, culture, and ecology.
The study will cover seven other river basins—Anseongcheon, Sapgyocheon, Mangyeong, Dongjin, Tamjin, Taehwa, and Hyeongsan—whose rivers are closely connected to local residents' lives and regional development. Rather than the piecemeal river works carried out to date, it will develop a comprehensive implementation plan, like the Four Rivers Restoration Project, to revive rivers' key functions in flood control, water use, the environment, and culture.
* Korea has 61 national rivers (3,002 km). Eighteen (1,973 km) are included in the Four Rivers Restoration Project. This study will prepare plans for the remaining 43 national rivers (1,029 km).
Along with launching the study, the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs plans to consult the relevant ministries, including the Ministry of Environment, the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, and the Ministry of Culture, as well as the local governments concerned. In connection with river works, it will also develop plans for water-quality improvement and a range of regional development initiatives involving culture, tourism, and leisure. In particular, the Mangyeong and Dongjin rivers will be directly linked to the government's Saemangeum Master Plan, now under development, to establish a foundation for the project's successful implementation, including improving water quality in Saemangeum and creating an ecological belt.
In connection with planning for national rivers, the Ministry is also preparing improvement plans for the smaller local rivers that flow into them. It said that when the master plan is completed in December 2010, comprehensive improvement plans will be in place for all rivers nationwide.

ko-news-notices-431-8372c75064.title: Tidal-Current Renewable-Energy Resource Map at a Glance
ko-news-notices-431-8372c75064.text:
Tidal-Current Renewable-Energy Resource Map at a Glance
2022-03-02
The National Oceanographic Research Institute has produced a renewable tidal-current energy resource map that lets users view tidal-energy information for the West and South coasts at a glance.
Tidal-current energy is an environmentally friendly energy source generated by installing water turbines where currents are strong. The study found high development potential along the West and South coasts, where tidal movements are pronounced.
The resource map was compiled by analyzing long-term seawater-flow data collected over the past 25 years at 337 locations from Baengnyeongdo to Ulsan.
The study found that the area with the highest energy density along Korea's coasts is near Uldolmok in Jeollanam-do, where a tidal-current power plant was completed on May 14 (27.8 MWh/m²). Next was the Gyodong Channel at the Han River estuary in Gyeonggi Bay (16.1 MWh/m²).
Other areas with high energy-density values were Maenggol Channel (15.1 MWh/m²), Geocha Channel (9.3 MWh/m²), and Jangjuk Channel (8.8 MWh/m²) in Jeollanam-do, and Daebang Channel (7.2 MWh/m²) in Gyeongsangnam-do.
The study, the first of its kind in Korea based on observation data, is expected to support green-energy development. It is also expected to help marine renewable-energy companies and research institutions conduct field tests of generating facilities, select suitable installation sites, and install equipment.
The Institute plans to keep providing updated information through its website (www.nori.go.kr), using ocean-observation data collected annually.

ko-news-notices-436-8372c75064.title: Equipment Installation Completed for Ulsan Port Seawater-Current Observation System
ko-news-notices-436-8372c75064.text:
Equipment Installation Completed for Ulsan Port Seawater-Current Observation System
2022-03-02
(Project carried out by our company)
Reporter Go Eun-hee — Ulsan Port Authority (UPA; President Lee Chae-ik) announced on the 9th that, over three days from August 4 to 6, it had completed installing equipment for the ‘Seawater-Current Observation System’ at Ulsan Port.
UPA invested about KRW 300 million in the system and worked jointly with the National Oceanographic Research Institute. The system consists of one set of meteorological-observation equipment, two real-time marine-observation units, and one seabed-moored marine-observation unit. They were installed at three locations: two in the waters in front of Ulsan New Port in Yongyeon-dong, Nam-gu, and one in the waters in front of the southern breakwater in Onsan-eup, Ulju-gun.
After testing the observation data this week, UPA will begin providing port users, through the National Oceanographic Research Institute website, with real-time information on currents and weather conditions in Ulsan Port, along with sea-level information from the existing Ulsan tide gauge station.
UPA plans to build a long-term data record through current observations in areas experiencing anomalous currents, analyze the causes of those currents through spatiotemporal analysis and numerical modeling, and use the results to support safe vessel operations.
UPA President Lee Chae-ik said, ‘We expect this system to help ensure the safety of vessels entering and leaving Ulsan Port. We will continue to do our best to make Ulsan Port safe.’
